detail.abstract: This work examines how Artificial Intelligence is being adopted across European public administrations, using the Public Sector Tech Watch (PSTW) dataset compiled by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre as an empirical foundation. Through a descriptive and exploratory analysis of 1,805 AI-related cases, the analysis examines patterns of adoption across countries and regions, the distribution of AI capabilities across government sectors, and the impacts that AI deployments are reporting in practice. The findings show that AI adoption is geographically concentrated in Western and Northern Europe, with Learning-based systems dominating across most sectors. Internally-focused deployments are slightly more common than citizen-facing ones, yet service-related impacts are the most frequently reported, suggesting that internal modernization often translates into tangible improvements in public service delivery. Governance-related impacts, such as transparency and public participation, remain comparatively marginal. The analysis also reveals significant documentation gaps around GovTech participation, pointing to a broader limitation in how public sector AI initiatives are currently reported. Overall, the results offer a data-driven snapshot of where AI stands in European public administration today.

title: The Compliance Evidence Gap: Why AI Governance Frameworks Stop Short at the Point of Proof
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Compliance Evidence Gap: Why AI Governance Frameworks Stop Short at the Point of Proof
detail.abstract: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the most detailed AI regulation any major economy has enacted, and it is precise about what an organisation deploying a high-risk system must demonstrate. It is almost silent on how the truth of that demonstration is to be tested. Article 12 requires high-risk systems to record their events automatically, but specifies no way to establish, later, that those records are genuine. The quality management obligation is met by written policies, and for most high-risk systems conformity is self-assessed, with no notified body and no independent audit. This article names the resulting defect the compliance evidence gap: a shortfall at the point of proof rather than at the point of obligation, and one distinct from the better-studied problem of verifying model behaviour. It maps the gap across the operative provisions of the Act, and shows that the leading certifiable assurance standard, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, inherits the same documentary model. The gap, the article argues, is best understood as missing infrastructure, to be built beneath the existing obligations rather than legislated on top of them.

detail.title: Some Simple Economics of Valuing Pre-training Data

detail.abstract: The standard objection to data compensation is that assigning value to individual data points is computationally infeasible at the scale of modern training. We argue that this objection is weaker than it appears because the training process already produces useful valuation signals. In particular, optimized data mixtures reveal information about the relative value of broad data sources, while scaling laws provide a benchmark for the aggregate share of model value attributable to data. We formalize the mixture-weight argument in a simple statistical model with correlated observations within sources and independent observations across sources, showing that, under a homoskedastic benchmark, optimal mixture shares equal relative information-value shares. We then extend the argument to neural-network training and characterize the corrections needed when data sources have heterogeneous return curves. Finally, we use standard scaling-law estimates to derive an upper-end benchmark for the aggregate data share of AI value. The result is a practical framework for coarse data valuation: use scaling laws to size the data pie, use optimized mixtures to divide it across sources, and route payments through a collective-management institution capable of aggregating claims.

title: Training AI For When Humans Will Use It
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and University of Toronto - Strategic Management

detail.title: Training AI For When Humans Will Use It
detail.abstract: AI predicts; humans use its predictions to make decisions. These predictions are combined with human verification and analysis, queries to other statistical models, and so on. The economic value of an AI, therefore, depends on how it interacts with the surrounding decision environment. We describe the value of AI as part of this "composite experiment" where AI makes a coarse prediction of the state of the world, show what this means for optimal model training via a geometric argument, explain why optimal training can be discontinuous in economic variables, and study how heterogeneous users or monopoly model trainers affect these results. In particular, maximizing the unconditional accuracy of AI predictions is generally suboptimal.

detail.abstract: AI investment decisions are increasingly made under conditions in which technology capabilities, platform boundaries, vendor offerings, and organizational readiness evolve faster than conventional planning cycles. Routine AI tool adoption can often be assessed through familiar ROI, payback, or productivity logic. The harder problem arises when a decision involves meaningful commitment: integration burden, execution delay, vendor dependency, architectural lock-in, process redesign, or exposure to platform substitution. In these situations, managers rely on experienced judgment. Advisors and senior leaders may sense that a proposal is too early, structurally weak, insufficiently recoverable, difficult to execute, or vulnerable to future platform absorption. Such judgment can be valuable, but when it remains implicit it is difficult to inspect, challenge, replicate, or improve. The problem is not that expert intuition exists; it is that many organizations lack a practical way to convert experienced judgment into an evidence-governed decision process. This working paper argues that AI commitment decisions require a disciplined middle ground between informal expert opinion and false quantitative precision. Drawing on structured expert judgment, strategy under uncertainty, real options reasoning, dynamic capabilities, AI adoption research, AIassisted decision-making literature, and recent practitioner guidance on AI investment and agentic AI, it proposes that managers structure these decisions around four questions: whether the opportunity is meaningful, whether enough value can be recovered, whether the organization can execute and absorb the change, and whether the commitment remains viable as the market evolves. The paper does not present a predictive model. Its purpose is to outline a practical decision discipline that makes expert judgment more explicit, evidence-constrained, and usable by managers who may not have an experienced advisor in the room.

detail.abstract: Generative and agentic AI have sharply lowered the marginal cost of producing knowledge-work outputs such as reports, presentations, code, copy, research summaries, and operational plans. Yet the diffusion of AIenabled speed has not automatically produced proportional organizational performance gains. This paper develops the concept of efficiency inflation to explain this gap. Efficiency inflation occurs when AI expands the volume and apparent completeness of professional output faster than organizations can increase the human judgment, contextual understanding, verification discipline, and accountability embedded in that output. Under such conditions, ordinary output becomes abundant and loses its premium, while high-density judgment becomes more scarce and more valuable. The paper advances a conceptual model in which the perceived value of a unit of professional output depends on the relationship between judgment density and output abundance. It integrates public enterprise surveys, labor-market signals, and organizational theory to identify five mechanisms: output commoditization, hidden supervisory labor, verification failure, cognitive-load transfer, and apprenticeship collapse. The paper further argues that AI is not simply replacing work, but repricing work by separating low-judgment execution from high-judgment responsibility-bearing. This is a theory-building working paper rather than a causal empirical study. Its contribution is to translate fragmented evidence on AI productivity, worker exhaustion, skill shifts, and organizational redesign into a coherent management theory for AI-augmented organizations. The proposed implication is that firms should not manage AI adoption primarily by output volume or task-speed metrics. They should redesign work systems to measure decision quality, evidence discipline, trust formation, and the preservation of human learning pathways.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital ecosystems has intensified regulatory scrutiny regarding the "dual role" of digital platforms, with ongoing debates over whether platform owners' entry into their own platforms suppresses third-party competitors. Using a stacked Difference-inDifferences approach and a comprehensive panel dataset, we evaluate the impact of Apple and Google's firstparty app launches on their most direct functional rivals. On Apple's iOS, first-party app entry immediately and significantly reduces direct rivals' downloads, revenues, and update frequencies, followed by a delayed decline in prices. Conversely, on the Google Play Store, platform entry yields no significant disruption to rivals' demand, pricing, or long-term innovation strategies. These findings highlight that the consequences of platform vertical integration are highly nuanced and ecosystem-specific, cautioning against broad, one-size-fits-all ex-ante regulations in favor of targeted, platform-level analyses.

title: Applicants Reactions to Artificial Intelligence in Hiring: A Narrative Review of Trust, Fairness, and Human-Centered Evaluation
affiliations: Middle Tennessee State University

detail.title: Applicants Reactions to Artificial Intelligence in Hiring: A Narrative Review of Trust, Fairness, and Human-Centered Evaluation
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into recruitment and selection processes, enabling organizations to automate resume screening, candidate ranking, interview assessment, and hiring recommendations. While AI offers substantial benefits in efficiency, scalability, and consistency, growing evidence suggests that applicants may react differently to AI-driven hiring procedures than to traditional human-driven approaches. Because hiring represents not only an assessment process but also an important organizational signal, applicants' reactions to AI can influence organizational attraction, application intentions, job acceptance decisions, and employer reputation. This narrative review synthesizes empirical studies examining applicants' reactions to AI use in recruitment and selection. The reviewed literature indicates that AI hiring is frequently associated with lower organizational attraction, reduced intent to apply, diminished trust, weaker procedural justice perceptions, lower social presence, and concerns regarding applicants' ability to demonstrate unique qualifications. However, the findings also suggest that applicants do not universally reject AI. Positive reactions emerge when AI systems are perceived as ethical, transparent, useful, and capable of reducing human bias. Drawing upon organizational justice theory, signaling theory, and human-AI interaction research, this review develops an integrated framework explaining how trust, procedural justice, communication quality, opportunity to perform, social presence, and uniqueness recognition influence applicant responses to AI-enabled hiring systems. Implications for future research and organizational practice are discussed.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted to appear in MIS Quarterly

detail.abstract: Paywalls that restrict access to online news content are essential for the sustainability of the institutional press in the digital age. However, there is little micro-level research on how readers respond when they encounter paywalls. For example, do readers respond by subscribing, by accessing non-premium content that is not behind the paywall, by circumventing the paywall, or by simply departing the website? We address this gap by using clickstream data from a major newspaper to study how readers respond to paywall encounters. This includes developing a novel method to detect when and how readers circumvent. We find that a key goal of presenting readers with the paywall-getting them to subscribe-is achieved only ~0.21% of the time. Despite this low conversion rate, the paywall is an effective nudge, as the likelihood that online readers subscribe without encountering it is far lower. Readers circumvent the paywall ~10% of the time, typically by using a new browser cookie likely generated by switching to private browsing mode. Readers of differentiated content and those who access the website directly are more engaged than other readers, as evidenced by their higher propensity to respond to the paywall by subscribing, circumventing, or accessing non-paywalled content. Newspapers and other publishers can use our results to enhance reader engagement and improve paywall design, e.g., by using our method to detect and respond to paywall circumvention.

title: Before the Law takes Effect: Provider Anticipatory Behavior
affiliations: Nova School of Business and Economics, New York University (NYU), Leonard N. Stern School of Business, Department of Management and Organizational Behavior, Students and Nova School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Before the Law takes Effect: Provider Anticipatory Behavior
detail.abstract: What if the market impacts of platform regulation begin before the law actually takes effect? While traditional hierarchical firms manage regulatory compliance through top-down mandates, digital platforms face a distinct vulnerability: autonomous supply-side users can preemptively alter their operations, causing immediate platform revenue losses before a law is even enforced. This paper explores how Airbnb hosts respond during the critical approval-to-enforcement window of short-term rental regulation. Using listing-level data from five U.S. cities, combined with ordinance requirements, we show that hosts reduce supply immediately after regulatory approval, well before formal enforcement begins. The decline is gradual, grows as enforcement approaches, and reduces platform revenue and realized bookings. We argue that regulation approval itself makes future operating constraints credible, prompting hosts to reassess whether their current routines can continue under the incoming rules. To test this mechanism, we construct a Regulatory Risk Index that compares each listing's pre-approval activity to the requirements of the regulation. Listings with higher regulatory risk reduce availability more strongly, especially along the margins directly targeted by regulation, such as multi-listing operation and high prior booking intensity. These early reductions also foretell post-enforcement sorting: listings that scale back more before enforcement are less likely to apply for a license and more likely to exit. Our findings show that anticipatory behavior is not merely a threat to identification or a pre-trend to be controlled away. It is a meaningful market response through which credible future regulation begins reshaping platform supply before enforcement formally starts.

title: Self-Improving Neural-Guided Pruning: A Graph Neural Network Framework for Scalable Mixed Bundle Pricing
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen,  and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: Self-Improving Neural-Guided Pruning: A Graph Neural Network Framework for Scalable Mixed Bundle Pricing
detail.abstract: Mixed bundle pricing is a classic revenue management problem arising in industries such as e-commerce, tourism, and video games. It refers to designing product combinations (i.e., bundles) and determining their prices to maximize expected profit. Exact mixed bundling models capture this structure but become computationally intractable because the number of candidate bundles grows exponentially with the number of products. We develop a graph neural network (GNN)-guided pruning-then-optimization framework for bundle pricing with (non-)additive valuations. The method represents each instance as a compact segmentproduct graph, predicts segment-product inclusion probabilities, and accordingly prunes the exponential bundle space into a small candidate family; the final prices and bundle offerings are obtained by solving the mixed bundling formulation over the retained bundles, possibly refined by a GNN-guided local search. Because exact labels are available only at small scales, we further propose an iterative self-improvement procedure: the current GNN policies generate high-quality solutions on large-scale instances, which serve as near-optimal labels for training a stronger model at larger scales. Theoretically, we show that under mild conditions the proposed edge-output GNN class is expressive enough to represent the optimal productassignment mapping, justifying the edge-level learning target. Numerical experiments show that the fastest proposed policy delivers 13-21% higher profit than bundle-size pricing on instances with up to 100 products at about 2% of its runtime. The framework shows when and why learning creates value in bundle pricing: prediction is used not to replace optimization but to identify where optimization effort should be concentrated, preserving the pricing rigor of exact mixed bundling while breaking its scalability barrier. As product catalogs grow beyond the reach of exact labels, the self-improvement procedure lets the deployed model generate its own retraining supervision, keeping the GNN maintainable at scale.

title: The SupTech Blueprint: DataStack Architecture for Consumer and Investor Protection

detail.title: The SupTech Blueprint: DataStack Architecture for Consumer and Investor Protection

declarations.funderStatement: Gates Foundation

detail.abstract:
Financial consumer and investor protection authorities have digitized faster than they have integrated. Complaint portals, disclosure-ingestion tools, and rule-based screening proliferate, yet most authorities plateau at foundation functions and don't reach sustained, production-grade. AI-powered supervisory intelligence. The binding constraint is rarely the absence of technology; it is architectural incoherence across the end-to-end supervisory pipeline.

This Manual is a build guide for closing that gap. It translates consumer and investor protection supervision (CIPS) mandates into a concrete DataStack design method — what to build, at which layer, and in what sequence — structured across five sequential layers (collection, validation and processing, storage, analytics, and data products) and two cross-cutting dimensions (access and interoperability, governance and explainability). Rather than scoring maturity as a single index, it assesses readiness dimension-by-dimension, identifies the binding constraints, and converts them into buildable specifications: data dictionaries, workflow definitions, interoperability patterns, and implementation sequencing.

The method is grounded in an empirical corpus of 102 deployed and prototyped supervisory solutions across consumer-facing authorities (e.g., CFPB, BSP, OJK, Banco de Portugal) and investor-facing securities and conduct authorities (e.g., CONSOB, ASIC, AMF Canada, U.S. SEC), with layer-by-layer reference architectures, workbook templates, and a four-phase implementation sequence calibrated to documented cost and time benchmarks.

It is the companion to SupTech-powered Consumer and Investor Protection Supervision: Architectural Pathway from Reactive Oversight to Outcome-Driven Institutional Intelligence: the Report establishes why authorities plateau and what works; the Manual specifies how to design the foundation-to-intelligence transition into a resilient, AI-ready architecture.

title: Determinants of Cyber-incidents among Small and Medium US Cities

detail.title: Determinants of Cyber-incidents among Small and Medium US Cities
detail.abstract: Cyber-incidents threaten the confidentiality, efficiency, and integrity of digital information systems, causing privacy risks, economic losses, and reputational damages, and exposing managerial limitations. Although these phenomena are becoming more frequent in public agencies, research to date has mainly focused on private sector organizations and individuals. In this study, we contribute to the broader literature on cyber-incidents by exploring the drivers of both security breaches and unauthorized data disclosures in public organizations. Drawing from routine activity theory, we develop hypotheses on the determinants of cyberincidents in departments in small and medium-sized US cities and test them using data from a national survey of public managers. Our findings suggest that both environmental and organizational factors are key determinants of cyber-incidents in city government. The results demonstrate the application of routine activity theory to public sector organizations and identify external and internal elements related to cyber-incidents in city government departments.

detail.abstract: Uniformly weighted divergence preferences (UWDP) introduced in Maccheroni et al. (2006) are an important class of risk-averse preferences that contain as a special case the monotone mean-variance utility. UWDP are characterised by the lowest expected value of an act in L ∞ under an adversarially chosen probability measure combined with the divergence of this measure. Our main result provides an alternative, computationally friendlier formula, which establishes in full generality that UWDP are the translation-invariant hull of state-independent expected utility over L 0. Some consequences of the new representation are studied.

title: Derivatives Funding Costs: XVA Reduction via Bond Decomposition

detail.title: Derivatives Funding Costs: XVA Reduction via Bond Decomposition
detail.abstract: We show that any uncollateralised OTC forward sale (resp. purchase) can be decomposed into a long escrow-secured put(resp. call) bond issued by the counterparty and a short partially margined call (resp. put) option traded bilaterally with the bank. The escrow is set to min(V Call , V Put), which the bank posts as variation margin on the bilateral call (resp put); the counterparty lodges this directly as escrow on the put bond, incurring no net cash outow. This escrow sizing exploits a generalised callput parity identity that eliminates the time-value penalty of a naive decomposition and reduces the residual default exposure to (-V Fwd) + resp. (V Fwd) +. Because the secured bond is repo-eligible, the bank can nance a back-to-back CCP hedge without creating unsecured funding needs; the net XVA reduces to CVA plus FBA with no funding cost adjustment (FCA). The construction extends to portfolios of uncollateralised forwards and swaps via a secured bond basket, achieving the standard netting-set CVA with no additional FCA. Under a conservative 25% haircut, numerical results for FX options show that funding savings are substantial accross the range of strikes (OTM, ATM and ITM)strikes except for deep OTM forwards, FCA falls well within the bid-ask spread of the underlying spot rate.

detail.abstract:
Background: Chronic low back pain is heterogeneous, yet most subgrouping approaches rely on patient-reported measures alone. We aimed to identify multidimensional phenotypes by jointly modelling patient-reported measures and structural findings.

Methods: In a cross-sectional analysis of 1066 adults with chronic low back pain (mean age 43·2 years; 57% female) from the Berlin Back Study, we did latent profile analysis using six standardised indicators: pain intensity, pain-related disability, and composite indices of psychological distress, fear-avoidance, lumbar degenerative findings (disc, facet, endplate), and stenotic or nerve-related MRI findings.

Findings: A four-profile solution provided the best balance of fit and interpretability (entropy 0·76; mean posterior probability 0·87). Three profiles (95·3%) showed graded severity on patient-reported measures with imaging composites near the sample mean: low (53·1%; mean pain 1·5/10), moderate (30·3%; 2·9), and high (11·9%; 4·3). A fourth profile (4·7%, n=50) was distinguished by elevated degenerative (z=2·0) and stenotic or nerve-related (z=0·9) findings despite low symptom severity (pain intensity 2·0/10); these participants were about 13 years older (mean 55·6 years), with two- to three-fold longer pain duration (median 15 vs 4–8 years; both p<0·001).

Interpretation: Jointly modelling patient-reported measures and imaging at scale resolved chronic low back pain into clinically interpretable phenotypes. These phenotypes provide a data-driven basis for stratifying care, and for interpreting imaging proportionately, particularly in older patients with pronounced structural findings but low symptom burden.Funding German Research Foundation (DFG) and German Aerospace Center (DLR).

detail.abstract:
Background: Non-laboratory-based cardiovascular risk calculators are essential in resource-limited settings. However, concordance between WHO/PAHO HEARTS and Globorisk-LAC remains unevaluated in vulnerable Latin American populations, such as older adults from the Peruvian Amazon.

Methods: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the AMAZON-FRAIL (168 cardiovascular disease-free adults aged 60–74 years; three Amazonian communities). Ten-year risk was categorized as low (<10%), moderate (10–<20%), or high (≥20%). Cohen’s κ and PABAK assessed categorical agreement; Pearson’s r, ICC, and Bland–Altman analysis assessed continuous agreement.

Findings: Mean 10-year WHO/PAHO score was 7·0% (SD 2·8) versus 12·1% (SD 4·4) for Globorisk-LAC (p < 0·0001). WHO/PAHO classified 82·1% as low and 17·9% as moderate risk; Globorisk-LAC classified 32·7%, 62·5%, and 4·8%, respectively. Overall categorical agreement was 45·8% (κ = 0·13, slight; PABAK = −0·08); moderate in males (κ = 0·43) but near-zero in females (κ = 0·01, slight). Pearson's r ranged 0·82–0·93; ICC was 0·38. Bland–Altman analysis revealed a systematic positive bias (overall mean difference 5·1 percentage points), with proportional widening at higher risk levels (slope p < 0·001).

Interpretation: Despite strong linear correlation, WHO/PAHO HEARTS and Globorisk-LAC are not interchangeable for cardiovascular risk categorization in older Amazonian adults, owing to systematic positive bias by Globorisk-LAC. Prospective outcome validation is required before either tool guides therapeutic allocation in this population.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to critique the criminalization of intellectual property. It will draw largely from references of counterfeiting, culture jamming and media piracy. It will also trace the history of brand identities, and logos to understand its social meaning. The social aspiration to experience luxury, prestige, and status associated with the brands transforms criminalization into a tool to limit accessibility and preserve brand values. Counterfeiting, culture jamming and media piracy resist corporate culture through which the existence of social hierarchies in the semiotic structure, becomes more apparent. The semiotics of logos will be examined to challenge the social distinction created through brand values. The elements of Mikhail Bakhtin's carnival have a significant contribution in understanding the ways in which consumers experience social relevance through these acts of subverting corporate dominance. Therefore, this paper will criticize the criminalization of intellectual property through cultural criminology. Previous studies have focused on the economic value of intellectual property. However this research precedes the commercial value of intellectual property to lay down its influence in social context. It will also discuss the future implications of artificial intelligence on personal and social aspirations of individuals.

detail.title: The Cost of Living with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression across 13 Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Pfizer Independent Grants for Learning and Change.

detail.abstract:
Background: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common and severe form of muscular dystrophy and imposes a substantial economic burden on patients, caregivers, and health systems. Despite the emergence of ultra-high-cost disease-modifying therapies, no global pooled estimate of annual direct costs exists. We aimed to synthesise evidence on annual direct costs in DMD and identify sources of between-country cost variation.

Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting annual direct costs in DMD. Fourteen databases were searched from inception to May 2, 2025. Eligible studies, published from 2015 onwards in six languages, included confirmed DMD populations (≥10 participants) and extractable annual cost data. Costs were converted to purchasing power parity-adjusted US dollars. Random-effects models using restricted maximum likelihood estimated pooled annual costs. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 and τ2. Meta-regression evaluated GDP per capita, insurance system type, mean age, and ambulatory status. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were performed.

Findings: Seventeen studies (8 publications) including 4,697 individuals from 13 countries were analysed. The pooled annual direct cost of DMD was US$31,619 (95% CI: US$21,522–46,452). Heterogeneity was substantial (I2≈99%; τ2=0.589), although pooled estimates remained stable across sensitivity analyses (US$29,904–36,444). GDP per capita was the strongest predictor of costs (R2=47.4%; p=0.003), followed by insurance system type (R2=32.8%; p=0.020), with public systems associated with lower costs. Lower-GDP countries had markedly lower costs (US$20,129; 95% CI: US$11,491–35,260) than higher-GDP countries (US$49,617; 95% CI: US$36,090–68,214).

Interpretation: The annual direct cost of DMD is substantial and highly heterogeneous, reflecting national income and health system structure as much as disease severity. These findings provide a global economic benchmark for health technology assessment and reimbursement decisions in the era of high-cost DMD therapies.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that intellectual ability is an emergent property of systems, not individual models. Drawing on systems engineering, distributed cognition, and AI deployment research, it demonstrates that no single large language model can exhibit stable intellectual behavior without orchestration layers for memory, delegation, escalation, and control. These capabilities are not peripheral to intellectual behavior-they constitute it. The paper introduces the orchestration boundary as the primary unit of analysis for evaluating intellectual ability in deployed systems and reframes progress in AI as a systems integration problem rather than a model scaling problem.

detail.abstract: Accuracy-based evaluation dominates AI assessment, yet accuracy is a property of outputs, not of the processes that produce them. A model that achieves 90% on a benchmark by exploiting surface heuristics has not demonstrated the same intellectual capability as one that achieves 90% through principled compositional reasoning-and current evaluation frameworks cannot distinguish these cases. This paper proposes the capability-completeness criterion: a four-dimensional specification of AI intellectual ability grounded in cognitive science that distinguishes isolated task performance from compositional competence. The four required dimensions are compositional integration, calibrated persistence, distributional robustness, and calibrated uncertainty. The criterion makes no claims about consciousness or strong AGI; it is defined entirely in terms of measurable functional behavior. Its adoption changes what counts as AI progress. Across this series, the full capability set is memory, delegation, escalation, persistence, and system-level control; this paper treats calibrated persistence as one of four capability dimensions, not the full capability set named across the series.

title: Winners Glide, Losers Stumble: A Behavioral Reversal Tilt to Momentum
affiliations: and

detail.title: Winners Glide, Losers Stumble: A Behavioral Reversal Tilt to Momentum
detail.abstract: Winners trend up smoothly, but losers fall in fits and starts, punctuated by technical rebounds that revert. This asymmetry makes the short (loser) leg the weak, crash-prone side of crosssectional momentum: losers bounce, and the bounces are where a short position bleeds. This paper studies a parameter-free factor that exploits the asymmetry by tilting the short leg toward the rebounds it should fade. The factor is classic momentum, which skips the most recent month, multiplied stock by stock by that month's gross return, (1 + r) M. Across a century of U.S. common stocks and twelve international markets, this reversal-tilted factor outperforms classic momentum, and the entire improvement is on the short leg. The premium is not subsumed by standard factors, including the short-term-reversal factor, and it mitigates rather than amplifies momentum crashes. Because it lives in the smaller-capitalization stocks where reversal escapes arbitrage, its magnitude is modest once made tradable: the gross premium, large in the equal-weighted full universe whose absolute levels we do not interpret, narrows to roughly one to two percent per year in the shortable small-to mid-cap range, and to the smaller of those names in recent decades. The contribution is a precise, parameter-free upgrade to momentum's short leg, honestly bounded in size, not a large standalone alpha. The gain comes from how the recent month scales momentum, that is, from its interaction with the loser's downtrend, not from the recent return itself.

title: RAMP: Dual Momentum for Smarter Investing: A Volatility-Scaled, Drawdown-Controlled Equity Strategy

detail.title: RAMP: Dual Momentum for Smarter Investing: A Volatility-Scaled, Drawdown-Controlled Equity Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper introduces and evaluates RAMP (Relative and Absolute Momentum Portfolio), a systematic, rules-based equity strategy that pairs absolute momentum (trend-regime filters on broad indices) with relative momentum (cross-sectional ranking of individual stocks) and adds a volatility-scaled position-sizing overlay based on the Average True Range (ATR). Using survivorship-bias-free Norgate data and the RealTest backtesting engine over January 1994-December 2025, RAMP is evaluated on the Nasdaq-100 universe against a buy-and-hold benchmark. The dual-momentum engine alone compounds at 24.9% per year with a maximum drawdown of-33.4%, versus 13.9% and-82.9% for buy-and-hold. Adding the ATR overlay lowers the maximum drawdown by a further ∼44% to-18.8% and raises the Sharpe (1.06) and Sortino (1.73) ratios, while cutting average market exposure to ∼55%-at a cost of roughly six percentage points of annualized return. Across the dot-com bust, the global financial crisis, and the 2022 bear market, RAMP preserved capital and often compounded positively while the index fell sharply; the lone exception is the V-shaped 2020 recovery, where the strategy's de-risking lagged the rebound. The evidence characterizes ATR volatility scaling as a risk-management overlay that exchanges a portion of return for materially lower drawdowns and higher risk-adjusted performance, making RAMP well suited to long-horizon, tax-advantaged accounts.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a bounded public company extension of Cultural Asset Economics (CAE). It does not propose “CAE for stocks.” It proposes a CAE derived enterprise continuity review: a pre-valuation diagnostic for identifying structural continuity assumptions that may sit beneath public company analysis.

A public share may be liquid, standardized, continuously priced, and transferable. In that narrow sense, public equity ownership may approximate reversible portfolio exposure. The enterprise behind the share, however, may depend on structural conditions that are not equally reversible: leadership transferability, governance architecture, control continuity, institutional legibility, ownership friction, transition pathways, strategic system exposure, or recognition convertibility.

Public company valuation often assumes that the enterprise will remain coherent enough for future cash flow forecasts to matter. It assumes that leadership quality, governance, control, institutional role, recognition, and transition architecture remain sufficiently stable or transferable over the valuation horizon. CAE does not replace valuation, but it isolates selected structural assumptions that valuation and strategy may otherwise treat as background conditions.

The central claim can be stated plainly: public equity research often models companies as more reversible, transferable, and structurally coherent than the enterprises behind those public shares may actually support. CAE’s contribution is not the invention of entirely new variables, but the organization of continuity, ownership friction, transferability, and recognition convertibility into a non-aggregative structural diagnostic before valuation. A public share may be reversible, but the enterprise behind it may not be.

title: Digital Transformation, Productivity and Growth: Effects of AI and Broadband Infrastructure Adoption in the European Union
affiliations: WU Vienna University of Economics and Business,  and Institute for Industrial Research (IWI), Vienna University of Economics and Business - Institute for Production Management

detail.title: Digital Transformation, Productivity and Growth: Effects of AI and Broadband Infrastructure Adoption in the European Union
detail.abstract: This study investigates the effect of broadband infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption on labour productivity across the EU-27 from 2019 to 2025. Grounded in Romer (1990) endogenous growth theory and Rogers (2003) diffusion of innovations theory, the study employs a two-way fixed-effects panel regression stratified by initial productivity levels. The results indicate that fibre-to-the-premises (FTTP) penetration consistently drives productivity across all Member States, confirming its role as a foundational enabler. However, AI adoption presents a "productivity paradox". In lower-income states, the standalone effect of AI is significantly negative, likely due to high implementation costs and structural disruption. Crucially, the interaction between broadband and AI reveals a significant complementary effect for these states; broadband infrastructure acts as a moderator that mitigates AI's negative effects and facilitates productivity gains. In contrast, high-income states exhibit "infrastructure saturation", where the interaction between broadband and AI is not statistically significant. These findings suggest that while broadband is universally beneficial, capturing the benefits of AI in catch-up economies depends critically on infrastructure readiness. Policy should therefore prioritise integrated digital strategies to prevent economic divergence within the Union.

detail.abstract:
This article develops Regulatory Attention Allocation Theory (RAAT), a constitutional framework for understanding how regulatory agencies decide which risks receive attention and which remain ignored. It argues that attention-allocation decisions are not merely administrative choices but constitutionally significant exercises of public power because they determine which harms receive regulatory protection.

Existing scholarship has examined regulatory failure, accountability, and risk-based regulation, yet has paid insufficient attention to the accountability implications of regulatory inattention. To address this gap, the article proposes the Regulatory Attention Statement (RAS), a structured mechanism requiring regulators to explain priority choices, disclose deprioritised risks, identify potential blind spots, and justify reassessment decisions.

Drawing on constitutional theory, administrative law, parliamentary evidence, and UK regulatory practice, the article argues that greater transparency over attention-allocation decisions is necessary to strengthen accountability, democratic oversight, and regulatory legitimacy. It concludes that regulatory attention allocation should be recognised as a distinct form of public power subject to constitutional scrutiny.

title: Fiscal Crossroads: An Options Analysis of the City of Radford, Virginia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Fiscal Crossroads: An Options Analysis of the City of Radford, Virginia
detail.abstract: The City of Radford, Virginia is in formal fiscal distress. The Virginia Auditor of Public Accounts issued a preliminary fiscal-distress determination in November 2025 and, in March 2026, recommended state assistance to the Governor and the General Assembly. This independent options analysis, built entirely from city budgets, audited financial reports, council minutes, and Auditor of Public Accounts correspondence, diagnoses how Radford reached this position and lays out the paths available to it. The central finding is structural: Radford's General Fund does not cover its own operations. In FY2024 it took in $25.43 million and spent $33.14 million, closing part of the gap with a $3.97 million transfer from the city's municipal electric utility; even counting that transfer as revenue, the General Fund ran an operating shortfall of roughly $3.74 million. Four forces explain the trajectory: a sustained gap between revenue and expenditure across FY2011-FY2024, depletion of the Electric Fund as a covert General Fund subsidy ($47.85 million in cumulative transfers), a bifurcated charter splitting the cash and books functions, and exposure on two special-act revenue-sharing agreements, including the 1978 Pulaski County agreement now under constitutional challenge. The report keeps description and inference distinct and treats every figure as reproducible from the appendices.

title: When the Operator Builds the Plant: The Google–CFS Power Purchase Agreement and What It Means for Virginia's Energy Market

detail.title: When the Operator Builds the Plant: The Google–CFS Power Purchase Agreement and What It Means for Virginia's Energy Market
detail.abstract: This independent case study documents the power purchase agreements between Google, Eni, and Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) for electricity from the planned 400-megawatt ARC fusion plant in Chesterfield County, Virginia, now named the Fall Line Fusion Power Station, and analyzes what operator-anchored generation means for the Commonwealth's energy market, ratepayer cost allocation, and data center infrastructure policy. It examines the commercial instruments themselves: Google's 200 MW agreement of June 30, 2025, the Eni offtake of September 22, 2025 valued by the parties at more than $1 billion, and the equity stakes both buyers hold in the developer. The report treats the deals as a mechanism for buying down technology risk with reputational and balance-sheet capital, and keeps the contract and the physics in the same frame. It tracks the binding constraints on delivery across three independent clocks: the SPARC demonstration's net-energy-gain schedule, the federal and state permit stack, and CFS's April 2026 entry into PJM's reformed interconnection queue, the first such application by a fusion developer to a major grid operator. It situates the bet against Virginia's conventional-generation backdrop, including the GS-5 large-load rate class, the contested Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center gas plant, Dominion's resource planning, record PJM capacity auctions, and the proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy by NextEra. Written to age well whether ARC delivers in the early 2030s or never, it allocates risk among operator, developer, utility, and ratepayer, and flags the boundaries of the public record.

detail.abstract: Temperature anomalies reduce manufacturing value added share in developing countries, but only where food-processing sectors rely heavily on domestic agricultural inputs. Using a two-way fixed effects panel of 60 countries over 2005-2015 and Leontief backward linkage coefficients from Eora26 input-output tables, we estimate an interaction coefficient of-1.93 (p = 0.012): countries near the sample mean backward linkage face a manufacturing response 0.60 percentage points more negative per 1°C than countries with negligible food-agriculture linkage. A mediation test shows little attenuation after controlling for agricultural GDP growth, consistent with input-supply disruption rather than rural-income effects. The effect concentrates in low-and lower-middle-income countries where food processors have limited ability to substitute imported inputs when domestic agricultural supply is disrupted. Placebo tests on sectors with near-zero agricultural linkage produce null results. Climate adaptation investment should reach domestic supply chains, not just farms.

title: We Don't Need the English: LA Punk, Cold War Sprawl, and the Limits of the Punk Canon
affiliations: University of Puget Sound

detail.title: We Don't Need the English: LA Punk, Cold War Sprawl, and the Limits of the Punk Canon
detail.abstract: This article argues that first-wave Los Angeles punk was more than a late West Coast version of London or New York punk. Most punk histories have made London the story of spectacle, scandal, and the Sex Pistols, while New York has become the story of CBGB, downtown art, critics, and bohemian concentration. Greil Marcus's Lipstick Traces gave punk a deeper intellectual genealogy, tying it to Dada, Situationism, and European traditions of refusal. Los Angeles does not fit that story very well. Its punk scene was more scattered, moving through freeways, clubs, record stores, apartments, buses, police encounters, Chinese restaurant venues, and small labels. LA punk mattered because it revealed a different America: Cold War sprawl, youth movement, racial and ethnic mixture, fragile DIY institutions, immigrant business spaces, entertainment fantasy, police violence, and the everyday routes that made the scene possible. LA punk was not one room, one rupture, or one lineage. It was circulation: records in the mail, kids on buses, bands in temporary rooms, Chinatown venues, saints on dashboards, and nuclear dread folded into ordinary life.

detail.abstract: We introduce Kruskal projection, a deterministic O(m logm) algorithm that maps any continuous dual vector to a guaranteed valid spanning-tree basis for Network Simplex, transforming the infeasible discrete basis-prediction problem into unconstrained regression. We make a mechanistic discovery: HiGHS Network Simplex with presolve disabled starts from a bare zero basis, ignoring all crash heuristics; consequently, any injected spanning tree reduces iterations by over 40% on DAG-MCF instances. We train FlowGNN, a Softmin GCN predicting dual variables, achieving +33.0% iteration reduction in-distribution and +10.8% out-of-distribution (2× scale). We honestly disclose that a cost-dominated Kruskal baseline (+42.5%) and a Gasse GCN baseline (+66.8%) both exceed FlowGNN in-distribution, and that FlowGNN is catastrophically harmful at 4× scale (−83%). The Kruskal projection mechanism—not neural dual quality—is the primary driver of warm-start performance. All code, weights, and evaluation scripts are open-sourced.

title: The Effects of Absolute and Relative Schedule Quality on Frontline Retention and Performance

detail.title: The Effects of Absolute and Relative Schedule Quality on Frontline Retention and Performance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Technology & Operations Mgt. Unit Working Paper No. 27-004

detail.abstract: Using a combination of field and experimental data, we examine how absolute and relative schedule quality jointly shape employee turnover and firm performance in the restaurant industry. Leveraging detailed shift-level data from a large restaurant group, we develop a data-driven measure of schedule quality and show that turnover is predicted by both absolute schedule quality and relative comparisons to peers. Employees are significantly more likely to leave when their schedules are worse than those of coworkers, even after accounting for the absolute quality of their own schedules. Among employees with below-average schedules, reducing the gap between their schedules and those of their coworkers explains approximately 50% of the difference in exit probabilities. A controlled lab experiment provides causal evidence for this relationship, demonstrating that relative disadvantage reduces perceived fairness, lowers schedule ratings, and reduces intentions to stay. At the restaurant level, we find that scheduling fairness and average schedule quality operate as distinct levers: fairer scheduling is associated with lower turnover but has no detectable effect on operational performance, while higher average schedule quality is associated with significantly higher sales and modestly-higher tips. This pattern is consistent with strategic schedule allocation in the restaurants we study – better schedules go to employees who generate higher sales per guest, who are in turn less likely to leave. These findings highlight the importance of both absolute and relative schedule quality as distinct dimensions of frontline work design, with different implications for retention and performance.

detail.abstract: Managing electricity demand is critical for lowering the cost of electrified products, integrating intermittent renewables, and reducing grid expansion needs. With its often flexible demand, electric vehicle (EV) charging has long been considered a promising candidate, yet many managed charging programs have not scaled. We analyze why this is the case and identify several challenges to existing programs, focusing on two business models: smart electricity consumption (V1G) and demand response (DR). After grounding the analysis in a stylized model, we leverage a longitudinal dataset of over 20,000 EVs and 1.5 million charging events across the U.S. to empirically study managed charging. We find that V1G with time-of-use pricing saves EV owners up to $300 annually but increases the utility's wholesale generation cost, a misalignment that in 75% of markets cannot be costs-effectively eliminated by paying owners to adjust charge timing. For DR, the top 10% of customers provide 5.2 times the average vehicle's value, and only 9.4% of vehicles can be profitably enrolled. We identify which charging behaviors predict profitable DR customers and how this interacts with utilities' prices. We further analytically show when V1G and DR may be misaligned, and show empirically that V1G participation cannibalizes 16-46% of DR returns, highlighting challenges with stacking value streams. Our findings help EV manufacturers decide which programs to offer, in which markets, and which customers to target or behaviors to incentivize. We highlight where utilities and regulators should adjust tariffs to better align EV owners' incentives with market outcomes.

title: Conceptualizing "Carbodollar": China's Structural Leverage in the South Korean EV Battery Supply Chain and Implications for East Asia

detail.title: Conceptualizing "Carbodollar": China's Structural Leverage in the South Korean EV Battery Supply Chain and Implications for East Asia
detail.abstract: How does China's dominance in the South Korean electric vehicle (EV) battery supply chain translate into political leverage without explicit threats or coercion? This thesis introduces the concept of carbodollar power to answer this question. Defined as the structural political-economic leverage a state acquires from controlling critical nodes within global decarbonization value chains, carbodollar power synthesizes three International Political Economy (IPE) traditions: Susan Strange's structural power (control over production and finance), Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye's asymmetric interdependence (vulnerability as the mechanism of leverage), and Robert Cox's Gramscian hegemony (durable power through consent). The framework analyzes power across three dimensions: productive (manufacturing and mineral processing), financial (green investment and development finance), and infrastructural/standard-setting (physical networks and technical rules that lock in dependence). Applying this framework to the South Korean EV battery supply chain, with Japan as a secondary comparison, this thesis finds that China's 80-96 percent control over critical battery inputs creates not mere sensitivity but structural vulnerability for South Korean firms, who operate without affordable alternatives. This vulnerability exhibits emerging hegemonic character: Chinese supply chains and technical standards now function as the taken-for-granted default for corporate strategy and policy calculation. The findings suggest that carbodollar power is reshaping East Asian regional order, constraining traditional developmental state strategies and forcing neighboring economies into managed vulnerability rather than autonomy. The thesis contributes to IPE theory by extending Strange's framework to the green transition, operationalizing vulnerability as the mechanism of leverage, and applying Gramscian hegemony to emerging green supply chains.

title: Security Challenges and Solutions in 5G and 6G Networks

detail.title: Security Challenges and Solutions in 5G and 6G Networks
detail.abstract: The study examines security threats and countermeasures within 5G and future 6G communication networks, highlighting the changing nature of cyber threats, vulnerabilities in the architecture, and future security mechanisms. With the hugely complex nature of networks, very low latency requirement, and the integration of tremendous Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the attack surface in modern communication systems has become significantly larger (Jahankhani et al. 2023). The literature-based synthesis method is used in the research to study the latest developments in network security, such as protection mechanisms based on artificial intelligence (AI), the use of techniques for physical-layer security, approaches for quantum-resistant networks, and the use of distributed security frameworks to increase robustness and scalability (Fakhouri et al. 2023). Persistent and emerging threats include edge computing vulnerabilities, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-enabled manipulation risks in future 6G environments (Mao et al. 2023). Although 5G networks have implemented better authentication methods and increased encryption methods, they still have significant drawbacks in terms of scalability, heterogeneity management for devices, and exposure in the IoT environment (Jazyah 2023). By contrast, 6G designs are likely to feature more AI-enhanced security patterns and features, such as AI-native security systems, blockchain-based trust management, and intelligent physical-layer defenses, that will enable adaptive and self-healing security capabilities (Shen et al. 2023). The researchers believe that a combination of AI-powered analytics, quantum-resistant cryptographic techniques, and a decentralized architecture will be essential to the future of secure and resilient networks. This is an important way to ensure that communication infrastructures in the future digital space will be trustworthy, scalable, and sustainable (Mangla et al. 2023).

title: Exclusive Competence Without Comprehensive Legislation: The Constitutional Deficit in the Treatment of Third-Country Economic Operators in EU Public Procurement
affiliations: University of Zagreb Faculty of Law

detail.title: Exclusive Competence Without Comprehensive Legislation: The Constitutional Deficit in the Treatment of Third-Country Economic Operators in EU Public Procurement
detail.abstract: The CJEU confirmed in Kolin (C-652/22) and Qingdao (C-266/22) that third-country economic operator access to EU public procurement falls within the EU's exclusive competence under the common commercial policy, while establishing problematic transitional rules. Yet the EU has not exercised this competence comprehensively. This paper argues that the result is a constitutional deficit. Drawing on pre-emption under Article 2(1) TFEU, the effectiveness of the common commercial policy, sincere cooperation under Article 4(3) TEU, and the right to effective judicial protection under Article 47 CFREU — the paper demonstrates that this deficit is incompatible with the constitutional principles that justify the conferral of exclusive competence. It proposes a four-element legislative framework: transparent admission discretion, mandatory score adjustments within a legislated range, removal of the undefined 'differential treatment arrangements' that paragraph 64 of Kolin establishes, and full public procurement remedies for admitted third-country operators as required by Article 47 CFREU.

title: AI-Driven Intrusion Detection System for Zero-Day Attack Prevention

detail.title: AI-Driven Intrusion Detection System for Zero-Day Attack Prevention
detail.abstract: Zero-day attacks are the ones that rely on vulnerabilities that have not yet been discovered, revealing new vulnerabilities and then exploiting them before security patches are released. Cyber threats are rapidly evolving, resulting in a surge in sophistication and frequency of zero-day attacks. The attacks are a significant threat to organizations, as traditional security measures are not able to identify the attacks in a timely fashion. The traditional signature-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) can only detect known attacks and attack patterns, and have a limited effectiveness when it comes to novel and emerging attack vectors. In this context, researchers and practitioners in the field of cybersecurity have begun to adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods to improve their threat detection and response abilities. This research work explores the effectiveness of AI based IDS techniques in overcoming traditional detection system's shortcomings. The research is based on the existing literature and empirical results of several recent studies (Por et al.; Tariq, Tariq, and Lu; Olaoye; Alansary et al.), and compares the IDS models using machine learning and deep learning techniques with traditional signature-based IDS models. The analysis will concentrate on important metrics such as accuracy of detection, false positives, response time and the capability of detecting new threats. The results suggest that AI-based IDS are more effective than traditional IDS in identifying complex and zero-day attacks. On the other hand, machine learning algorithms can outperform in pattern recognition, and deep learning models can be used in detecting abnormal network activities that could be a new threat. Additionally, AI-enriched systems are faster to respond and more powerful to predict threats, allowing proactive measures to be taken instead of reactive defense. This study's main value is the compilation of all available evidence of how important AI is in today's intrusion detection system strategies. The findings highlight the significance of adopting AI capabilities in cybersecurity systems to enhance their resilience against new cyber threats. In today's intricate digital landscape, organizations that embrace AI-powered IDS can bolster their security defenses, minimize threats, and improve the overall security of their networks.

title: Deep Learning Models for Malware Detection and Classification

detail.title: Deep Learning Models for Malware Detection and Classification
detail.abstract: The rapid evolution of malware, particularly polymorphic and zero-day variants, has significantly reduced the effectiveness of conventional signature-based and rule-driven detection systems. Recent advances in deep learning have created new opportunities for malware detection by enabling models to automatically learn complex feature representations from raw or transformed data. This study presents a comparative analysis of three deep learning architectures for malware detection and classification: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and a Hybrid CNN-LSTM model. The objective is to evaluate how effectively these architectures capture spatial and sequential patterns in malware data while balancing detection accuracy, robustness, and practical applicability. The comparative results reported in the manuscript show that the Hybrid CNN-LSTM model outperforms the standalone CNN and LSTM models across all evaluation metrics, achieving 96% accuracy, 95% precision, 94% recall, and a 94.5% F1-score, compared with 92%, 91%, 90%, and 90.5% for CNN, and 89%, 88%, 87%, and 87.5% for LSTM. The findings suggest that combining structural and behavioral feature learning can improve malware classification performance. At the same time, the study identifies persistent challenges related to dataset imbalance, interpretability, computational cost, and real-world deployment. Overall, the paper argues that hybrid deep learning architectures provide a promising direction for next-generation malware detection systems, particularly in complex environments such as Android and IoT ecosystems.

title: Cybersecurity Risk Assessment Models for Critical Infrastructure

detail.title: Cybersecurity Risk Assessment Models for Critical Infrastructure
detail.abstract: The study considers cybersecurity risk assessment models of critical infrastructure systems such as energy networks, industrial control systems, and smart utility systems that are subjected to ever-evolving cyberattacks. It integrates cutting-edge advancements in static, dynamic, predictive and AI based approaches for risk assessment and risk reduction for cyber threats in complex operational settings. Results shows that hybrid/Adaptive approaches outperform static approaches across interconnected systems in detecting, responding to and anticipating new threat vectors. By incorporating machine learning, ontological modeling and digital twin technologies, real-time situational awareness and advanced persistent threat resiliency are enhanced. Despite the many advantages, there are significant interoperability, scalability, data standardization and cross-framework issues that hinder seamless deployment in heterogeneous infrastructure ecosystems. The study suggests that cybersecurity resilience in the future will rely on "automated" and "context-aware" and "adaptive" systems for assessing risk that incorporate multi-layered intelligence and continuous learning mechanisms. In methodological terms, the study is a systematic synthesis of recent literature on cybersecurity risk modeling, with particular emphasis on the comparative evaluation of analytical, probabilistic and AI enhanced approaches to cybersecurity risk modeling in the different infrastructure domains. The implications suggest that there is a need for standardized frameworks which facilitate secure data sharing, better model interoperability and decision support in real time for operators of critical infrastructure resilience. Research areas for future work include improving the efficiency of computation of AI driven models, minimizing the number of false positives in anomaly detection, and improving the governance framework of cybersecurity risk management. The study overall presents a unified view of changing paradigms for the risk assessment of critical digital infrastructure against global persistent and emerging cyber threats in operational environments effectively.

title: The Swarm Accountability Gap in Autonomous Finance: Delegation Failure and Institutional Responsibility in Agentic Finance and Autonomous Financial Systems

detail.title: The Swarm Accountability Gap in Autonomous Finance: Delegation Failure and Institutional Responsibility in Agentic Finance and Autonomous Financial Systems

detail.abstract:
The rapid adoption of agentic and multi-agent AI systems in financial services exposes a governance shortfall that cannot be resolved by agent identity, orchestration, runtime security, payment authorisation, observability or model-level explainability alone. These layers increasingly address individual AI agent behaviour, communication, permissioning and technical verifiability. Yet none, by itself, resolves the institutional question at the centre of regulated finance: who remains accountable when interacting AI agents collectively produce a financial outcome?

This paper formalises the swarm accountability gap as the structural absence of governance at the interaction layer, where emergent financial outcomes arise. It develops delegation failure, introduced in Chaudhry (2026a), as the governance failure mode in which individually compliant agents, valid permissions, authenticated communications and clean technical traces collectively produce outcomes that no accountable human or institution clearly authorised, anticipated or can remedy. The paper distinguishes four concepts frequently conflated in practice: visibility, traceability, verifiability and accountability, arguing that the first three are necessary preconditions for the fourth but cannot substitute for it.

Drawing on the sharp acceleration of agentic finance through the first half of 2026, including the Financial Stability Board's consultation of 10 June 2026, which describes in substance the condition this paper identifies by name, the paper argues that technical governance is necessary but structurally insufficient. Institutional responsibility cannot be outsourced to platforms, protocols, vendors, models or agent swarms. It positions KYS: Know Your Swarm as the complementary institutional layer above existing technical governance, extending accountability from the individual AI agent to the collective financial outcome, and argues that the Gulf, and the United Arab Emirates in particular, is uniquely positioned to prototype this layer.

title: Policing Expressive Governance: A Framework for Judicial Review of Executive Viewpoint Retaliation
affiliations: Loyola Law School Los Angeles

detail.title: Policing Expressive Governance: A Framework for Judicial Review of Executive Viewpoint Retaliation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
The gravest contemporary threats to expressive freedom increasingly take the form not of statutes or criminal sanctions but of procurement decisions, grant terminations, security-clearance revocations, and regulatory designations — the discretionary instruments of executive administration. When the executive deploys these instruments to penalize disfavored viewpoints while preserving the appearance of ordinary governance, it engages in what I have elsewhere called expressive governance. The phenomenon is doctrinally elusive because it operates in domains where courts have long extended substantial deference to executive judgment, and because its defining features — facial neutrality, discretion, and post hoc justification — obscure the very motive the retaliation inquiry must locate.

This essay argues that existing First Amendment doctrine supplies the governing principles but lacks an administrable method calibrated to the low-visibility, discretion-cloaked form the problem now assumes, and it proposes such a method: three interlocking tools. First, a clear-statement requirement asks whether Congress authorized applying the discretionary instrument to domestic expressive activity or its infrastructure at all — a question of statutory reach, not of authority to discriminate by viewpoint, which Congress cannot confer. Second, a burden-shifting rule, triggered only by a conjunctive showing of a viewpoint-linked pattern and an exploitable dependency relationship, requires the government to prove on the record that it would have taken the same action for viewpoint-neutral reasons. Third, a presumption of systemic distortion heightens what the government must produce where the target is an expressive intermediary — an effect of burden allocation, not a new tier of scrutiny.

The essay develops the framework through the pending litigation over the Department of War's supply-chain-risk designation of a leading artificial-intelligence company, and tests it against the law-firm executive orders, public-broadcasting funding rescissions, press-credential revocations, and public employment and hiring. The method is politically symmetric by design: it operates on burden allocation and record evidence, gives the government a genuine path to prevail where its reasons are real, and equips courts to distinguish legitimate discretionary administration from viewpoint retaliation conducted through the routine machinery of the administrative state.

title: Ethical Risk Score: An Empirical Measure of Contractual Accountability and Discretion in U.S. Bank Executive Contracts

detail.title: Ethical Risk Score: An Empirical Measure of Contractual Accountability and Discretion in U.S. Bank Executive Contracts

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available corporate/regulatory filings and public market data only. It does not involve human participants, patient data, intervention, or identifiable private information. Institutional Review Board approval was therefore not required.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Ethical Risk Score (ERS), a rule-based contract-analytics measure of contractual accountability and managerial discretion in executive governance agreements. Using SEC Exhibit 10 filings, the study analyzes 288 executive compensation and governance contracts and 4,299 contractual clauses from 19 publicly traded U.S. banking institutions during 2022-2026. ERS identifies accountability-enhancing provisions, including clawbacks, recoupment rights, compliance obligations, forfeiture provisions, and regulatory requirements, as well as discretionenhancing provisions, including sole-discretion authority, indemnification protections, change-incontrol protections, and release-of-claims provisions. The results show substantial variation in contractual governance structures across banks. Preliminary validation indicates no meaningful relationship between ERS and short-term stock volatility, suggesting that ERS should be interpreted as a contractual governance measure rather than a market-risk measure. ERS is strongly associated with Governance Balance (r = 0.717; R² = 0.514), although this relationship primarily reflects internal consistency because both measures rely on related accountability and discretion categories. A small pilot enforcement analysis suggests lower average ERS scores among enforcement-associated observations, but the sample is exploratory and not statistically conclusive. The paper contributes a reproducible empirical approach for transforming legally binding executive contracts into structured governance data, and establishes a foundation for future research using larger enforcement datasets, SOX 404 internal-control measures, hand-coded clause validation, and machine-learning-based classification.

title: From Store to Surplus Food Platform: Implications of Competition in Quantity-Based Sales
affiliations: University of New Hampshire - Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics and California State University Fullerton

detail.title: From Store to Surplus Food Platform: Implications of Competition in Quantity-Based Sales
detail.abstract: On quantity-based surplus food platforms, retailers sell surplus bags containing the end-of-day leftovers from their stores. Each retailer's decisions on bag price, production quantity, and quantity reserved for surplus sales are complicated by: (i) interlink between reservation for surplus sales and ability to serve in-store sales, (ii) uncertainty in the leftover quantity while having to ensure a guaranteed minimum quantity for the bag, (iii) intricate relationships among different contextual factors (e.g., consumer consumption needs, consumer valuation of the bag, and platform discount rate), and (iv) competition among retailers. We identify conditions under which the retailer should increase the bag price to improve the profit margin on surplus bags and/or reduce unmet demand from in-store sales, highlighting the need to carefully balance retailer-, consumer-, and platform-specific factors. Interestingly, compared with a no-competition benchmark, competition can lead to a higher bag price, more food reserved for surplus sales, and less food available for in-store sales. More importantly, we offer three key insights regarding resulting outcomes. First, competition (versus no-competition) can yield higher consumer surplus, higher retailer's profit, and lower food waste (e.g., when the discount rate is low, and consumers' valuation of surplus bags is high). Second, intense competition can reduce retailer's profit and exacerbate food waste, suggesting that having more retailers may result in unintended consequences. Third, platforms can mitigate these consequences by leveraging the discount rate. For instance, in areas with many competing retailers and many consumers with small consumption needs, platforms should set the discount rate low.
