detail.abstract:
AIR9000 Phase 2, 4 and 6 â€” the MRH90 Taipan helicopter program â€” occupies a unique position in Australian
Defence acquisition history and in the Program Drift Theory research programme. It is the only major program in the
MPR series to be terminated rather than recovered: in September 2023, the Australian Government announced that
the MRH-90 helicopter fleet would not return to flying operations, with all 47 aircraft grounded and subsequently
disposed of. The MRH90 had been a Project of Concern continuously since November 2011 â€” a twelve-year period
from first POC listing to termination decision.
This paper analyses MRH90 as the terminal case in the ANAO Back-Test Series â€” the case that demonstrates what
Program Drift looks like when systemic conditions are not arrested and the program crosses the tipping point into self-
sustaining deterioration. Program Drift Theory (Lindemann, 2026b) proposes a specific and important theoretical
distinction: programs in pre-tipping-point deterioration can, in principle, be recovered through structural intervention;
programs that have crossed the tipping point into self-sustaining deterioration cannot be recovered through
conventional governance response. The MRH90 case tests this proposition empirically.
The analysis maps ANAO narrative findings across 12 MPR editions (2007-08 to 2022-23) against SEWI proxy
conditions, identifying when each condition first appeared, when conditions became self-reinforcing, and when the
program crossed the theoretical tipping point into irreversible deterioration. The analysis finds that SEWI conditions
were present from the earliest MPR appearances â€” from 2007-08 â€” and that the program crossed the tipping point
at approximately 2016-17, when the accumulated combination of technical debt, contractor remediation failure, and
governance normalisation of deviance produced conditions from which conventional recovery mechanisms could not
generate positive trajectory.
The MRH90 case provides the empirical foundation for Program Drift Theory's most important practical claim: that
early intervention â€” before tipping point conditions are crossed â€” is not simply preferable but structurally
necessary. The twelve-year period from POC listing to termination, at an estimated programme cost exceeding AUD 3.7
billion, documents the consequence of governance response that came after the tipping point rather than before it

title: Relative Wealth Command, Monetary Shares, and Incremental Allocation in Fiat Money Systems

detail.abstract: This paper develops a share-based framework for analyzing monetary non-neutrality in fiat money systems. Its central claim is not simply that money creation is distributional, but that the distributional significance of money creation begins at the point of initial allocation. The paper introduces Relative Wealth Command (RWC) as a framework for analyzing agents' relative monetary positions and the Incremental Allocation Mechanism (IAM) as the rule governing the distribution of newly created purchasing power. The key result is a simple share condition: relative monetary positions change whenever an agent's share in newly created purchasing power differs from that agent's pre-existing monetary share. This distinguishes the framework from Cantillon-type accounts, which emphasize transmission path and sequence, and from heterogeneous-agent redistribution analyses, which focus on the effects of monetary shocks after they enter the economy. In a two-agent model, the paper further shows that wealth shares can change through both the direct allocation of newly created purchasing power and asset-price revaluation. The main implication is that monetary expansion is not distributively neutral, and its first-round effects depend on how newly created purchasing power is initially allocated.

title: The Citizens Standard: External Interoperability and the Common Anchor
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Citizens Standard: External Interoperability and the Common Anchor
detail.abstract: The first six papers of the Citizens Standard (CS) specify a domestic monetary architecture. This paper closes the multilateral question: how CS economies — with different productivity levels, demographic profiles, and trade balances — interoperate when they operate side by side and must exchange goods, services, and claims. The design commitment is twofold. CS economies settle cross-border claims through a computed real-purchasing-power exchange layer: an exchange rate calculated from verifiable real data rather than traded in a market, and therefore without a speculative attack surface. (This class of settlement mechanism was introduced by Serra's EQUA; CS builds on that idea and specifies its own layer of the same class.) And CS members commit to a predictability standard: a credible, low-variance price path anchored at a common target of approximately zero inflation. The central result is that zero is the uniquely robust anchor. Heterogeneous national inflation levels distort the bilateral real rate under sticky wages; a common level reduces this, but a common positive level (such as a 2–4% corridor) leaves a residual whenever cross-country wage stickiness differs, while a common zero removes the inflation-driven distortion for every wage-adjustment process at once. Zero is, in addition, the cost-minimizing level and the non-arbitrary focal point. The domestic results are computed on the framework's actual issuance engine at its published launch calibration; the external-layer results are a calibrated property of the settlement layer's exact formula.

title: No Premium for PDFs: Field Heterogeneity and the Collapse of the "Format Advantage" Hypothesis in Urban Economics and Regional Science
affiliations: Central Bank of Armenia

detail.title: No Premium for PDFs: Field Heterogeneity and the Collapse of the "Format Advantage" Hypothesis in Urban Economics and Regional Science
detail.abstract: Do metadata prefixes such as [PDF] or [BOOK] signal a universal citation advantage, or are their effects artifacts of field heterogeneity and sparse labeling? Using a complete audit of the urban literature dataset (N=1,280 records equally split across regional science, urban amenities, and urban economics), I show that the often-claimed "PDF premium" disappears once the data are properly cleaned. Negative binomial regression with journal-clustered standard errors reveals that urban amenities entries receive 78.6% fewer citations than regional science entries (IRR=0.214, p¡0.001). Contrary to popular claims, the PDF prefix is associated with significantly lower citation rates relative to the Book baseline in the pooled model (IRR=0.418, p¡0.01). Type-specific models expose strong field heterogeneity: in urban economics, PDF shows IRR=0.283 (p¡0.01), while in regional science no prefix effect reaches significance. A zero-inflated negative binomial model confirms the findings, and a four-topic NMF on titles recovers the three literatures with high coherence. I conclude that "format premium" narratives are unsupported; instead, field membership and book-level publishing dominate citation patterns.

title: From Automation to Augmentation: A Human-Centered Framework for Responsible Generative AI in Education

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is changing how learners seek explanations, draft ideas, receive feedback, revise texts and complete academic tasks. Institutional responses tend to fall between two limited positions: viewing the technology mainly as a tool for automation and productivity, or mainly as a risk to academic integrity and independent learning. This article argues both views are incomplete, as the key educational question is whether generative AI helps or hurts human learning. The research employs a qualitative conceptual approach to differentiate between automation and augmentation, and to develop a human-centered model for responsible use in education, based on Self-Determination Theory. The discussion produces five key observations: that the responsible use of technology is a pedagogical matter, not a matter of tool presence; that augmentation has value when it supports autonomy, competence, and relatedness; that cognitive effort must be protected; that academic integrity involves process-sensitive assessment; and that institutional governance must link policy, pedagogy, professional development, and learner literacy. This article proposes a Human-Centered Augmentation Framework, which is oriented around six dimensions: pedagogical alignment, learner agency, cognitive effort, transparent process, relational teaching presence, and institutional accountability. This framework offers a practical way for educators and institutions to distinguish between learning-supportive and learning-substitutive use.

title: Current Account and Trade Balance Dynamics in a Schumpeterian Small Open Economy
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - Economics Department, Fairfield University and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Current Account and Trade Balance Dynamics in a Schumpeterian Small Open Economy
detail.abstract: This paper studies current-account and trade-balance dynamics in a small open economy with Schumpeterian innovation, firm entry, and finite-horizon households under two alternative views of the world, while maintaining an exogenous world interest rate. In the canonical intertemporal approach, where exports are treated as residual, net foreign assets and the trade balance are entirely demand-driven and insulated from innovation and growth dynamics. When exports are modeled as an autonomous source of demand, foreign assets become a forward-looking valuation variable jointly determined by export demand and the allocation of output among consumption, innovation, and firm entry. Through the valuation channel, external shocks, such as export-demand shocks and world interest rate shocks, affect firm size and, through Schumpeterian mechanisms, feed back into the economy's net foreign asset position and trade balance.

title: The Prospect Theory Formula
affiliations: Heidelberg University

detail.title: The Prospect Theory Formula
detail.abstract: We provide a comprehensive treatment of the prospect theory (PT) formula and its application to general probability distributions (discrete, continuous, or neither). We give eight versions of the PT formula and relate them through elementary proofs. Each formula nests a different expected utility (EU) formula and offers different views on PT's probability weighting, i.e., its use of distorted probabilities in place of objective ones. We argue that giving up the focus on finite ("lottery") distributions is not only more general but also more intuitive.

title: The Implication of GIS Mapping in Agriculture and Land Monitoring for Environmental Policy Development

detail.title: The Implication of GIS Mapping in Agriculture and Land Monitoring for Environmental Policy Development
detail.abstract: This study proposes an interdisciplinary, data-driven approach to understanding historical and future trends in plant biodiversity in Italian rewilded mountain areas. We produced spatially explicit assessments of vegetation change between 1990 and 2020 in three mountain protected areas spanning the Italian Peninsula: 1) Eastern Alps (Lagorai mountain range); 2) Northern Apennines (Foreste Casentinesi Monte Falterona e Campigna NP), and 3) Central Apennines (Velino Massif). The methodology included generalized dissimilarity modeling (GDMs) to model the dissimilarity of plant assemblages as a function of their geographical distances, ecological dissimilarities, and differences in land cover derived by remote sensing. After calibrating the GDMs with historical and newly collected vegetation plot data, the maps of predicted species composition at different times were created, and their comparison allowed highlighting areas where change in land cover induced the largest changes in species composition and quantifying the consequences for regional plant diversity.

detail.abstract:
This article is part of the "Internal Resistance" series within the broader "Economic
Guarantees of Security" (EGS) research program. The article develops the concept of
internal economic resistance as an integral, key, and measurable element of deterrence
against aggressive state policies.
Unlike traditional approaches to deterrence, which primarily rely on external military,
economic, financial, and political instruments, the proposed approach focuses on
transmitting the expected and actual consequences of aggressive policies into the
internal socioeconomic structure of the state.
The article introduces a distinction between the concepts of internal resistance as a
broad category of disobedience and economic resistance as its measurable component.
Thus, we transform a difficult-to-observe phenomenon (discontent, latent resistance,
loss of trust) into a system of observable economic reactions.
The concept and calculation method of the Resistance Index (R-Index) as a
measurement tool are proposed. The R-Index serves as an indicator of economic
resistance to state policies and as a measure of internal stability.
Regarding the development of a system of economic security guarantees (EGS), the
article concludes that a complete system of maintaining political equilibrium must
combine external economic, financial and political instruments with internal reactions
and behavioral resistance, thereby increasing the unacceptability and costs of
aggression.

title: Friends in Green Places: Political Incentives, Social Ties, and Corporate Green Governance in China
affiliations: , Central China Normal University,  and Peking University HSBC Business School

detail.title: Friends in Green Places: Political Incentives, Social Ties, and Corporate Green Governance in China
detail.abstract: We study how political leaders leverage social ties with subordinate officials to advance political objectives. Examining social ties between Chinese provincial leaders (party secretaries and governors) and environmental department directors, we show that such ties boost corporate green investment. Crucially, this effect is driven by governor-director ties, while secretary-director ties have no effect. This divergence stems from political incentives: environmental performance affects governors' promotions, prompting them to reward connected directors with higher promotion prospects for pollution abatement. Consequently, environmental enforcement strengthens, motivating firms to increase financing for green investment. Pollution emissions ultimately decline at both the firm and regional levels.

title: Does Financial Trading Smooth Non-Convex Markets?
affiliations: Max Planck Institue for Research on Collective Goods,  and Catholic University of Louvain (UCL) - Center for Operations Research and Econometrics (CORE)

detail.title: Does Financial Trading Smooth Non-Convex Markets?
detail.abstract: In non-convex markets, a competitive equilibrium may fail to exist. This turns out to be an important issue in real-world non-convex auction markets, such as electricity markets, as it complicates pricing and requires the auctioneer to resort to out-of-market discriminatory side payments to sustain an equilibrium. We investigate whether the introduction of convex financial trading induces a smoothing effect, mitigating the issues arising from non-convexities. We develop a two-stage non-convex market model (a forward market followed by a spot market) in which convex financial traders participate in the forward market. Our model predicts that financial trading reduces the magnitude of side payments required to support the cleared allocation. To test the prediction of our model, we examine the introduction of a transaction fee on financial traders in 2020 by PJM, the US's largest electricity market. We show that the substantial decline in financial trading volume caused by this policy coincided with a significant increase in side payments, in line with our theoretical predictions.

title: Eurogreen+: An Integrated Modelling Framework for Analysing Socioeconomic and Energy Transitions
affiliations: University of Pisa, University of Pisa, University of Pisa and University of Pisa

detail.title: Eurogreen+: An Integrated Modelling Framework for Analysing Socioeconomic and Energy Transitions
detail.abstract: Addressing climate change, ecological overshoot and persistent inequalities requires macroeconomic tools able to analyse transition pathways by integrating energy, distribution and structural change. This paper introduces Eurogreen+, a substantially revised version of the Eurogreen framework, and develops an empirically grounded baseline for Italy as a reference point for future policy analysis. The modelling framework combines post-Keynesian macroeconomics, stockflow consistent accounting, system dynamics and an open input-output production structure with endogenous, cost-driven technological change. Eurogreen+ fully integrates the economic and energy systems, features a high level of heterogeneity with 100 representative households differentiated by region and income quintile and explicitly accounts for supply constraints. Rather than evaluating specific policy packages, the paper presents the baseline scenario and a set of illustrative simulations to highlight central characteristics of the model. The baseline reproduces current trends of modest growth, insufficient emissions reductions, and rising labour-market inequality. The illustrative simulations show that Eurogeen+ captures hysteresis and the potential expansionary role of policy interventions. Moreover, the integrated representation of energy, technological change, consumption patterns reveal non-trivial interactions between emissions and distribution. Eurogreen+ thus provides an integrated empirical framework for analysing policy mixes aimed at promoting ecological transition and social cohesion with respect to the presented baseline.

title: Generative AI Mania and Macro Vulnerability: Asymmetric Volatility Dynamics of Tech Giants via EGARCH-X (2023-2026)

detail.abstract:
The period from January 2023 to July 2026 witnessed an unprecedented surge in investor enthusiasm surrounding generative artificial intelligence (AI), propelling technology-sector equities-most notably NVIDIA Corporation (NVDA)-to extraordinary cumulative excess returns. This paper examines whether the AI innovation narrative confers immunity to macroeconomic systemic risk transmission. Using 866 daily observations, we estimate Exponential GARCH models augmented with exogenous macro-stress variables (EGARCH-X), incorporating the ICE BofA MOVE Index as a proxy for sovereign bond market dislocation. Our cross-sectional analysis covers five assets: NVDA, AMD, MSFT, GOOGL, and the S&P; 500 (SPY). 
Three findings emerge. First, the leverage effect is monotonically weaker as assets move closer to the AI narrative core: SPY exhibits the strongest leverage (γ =-0.198, p < 0.001), while AMD shows no significant asymmetry (γ = +0.028, n.s.). This cross-sectional gradient is consistent with a behavioral hypothesis: momentum-driven buy-the-dip dynamics suppress the institutional fear-leverage channel in high-narrative assets. Second, NVDA's ARCH coefficient (α = 0.142) substantially exceeds SPY's (0.088), confirming greater sensitivity to information shocks. Third, a structural break analysis centered on the January 27, 2025 DeepSeek announcement reveals a fundamental regime shift in NVDA's volatility dynamics, while SPY parameters remain stable-evidence of AI-specific structural fragility.

title: Harnessing Predictive Analytics to Reduce Opioid Misuse, Opioid Use Disorder, and Overdose Deaths in the United States

detail.title: Harnessing Predictive Analytics to Reduce Opioid Misuse, Opioid Use Disorder, and Overdose Deaths in the United States

detail.abstract: The opioid epidemic remains one of the most significant public health challenges in the United States, contributing to substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditures. Although recent national surveillance has reported encouraging declines in overdose deaths, opioid use disorder (OUD) and opioid-related mortality continue to impose considerable burdens on healthcare systems and communities. Predictive analytics has emerged as a promising approach for improving opioid surveillance by identifying temporal patterns, forecasting future overdose trends, and supporting evidence-based public health interventions. This study examined national opioid overdose mortality trends using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) VSRR Provisional Drug Overdose Death Counts dataset. Records were filtered to include opioidinvolved overdose deaths (ICD-10 codes T40.0-T40.4 and T40.6) from 2015 through 2025. Following data cleaning and preprocessing, descriptive analyses, data visualization, Random Forest regression, feature importance analysis, and 12-month forecasting were performed using Python. The analysis identified substantial increases in opioid overdose mortality through 2023, followed by a notable decline during 2024 and 2025. The Random Forest model demonstrated that recent historical overdose mortality, particularly lagged mortality measures and rolling averages, were the strongest predictors of future opioid deaths. Forecasting suggested a continued downward trend in opioid mortality under current conditions, while emphasizing the uncertainty associated with changing drug markets, policy interventions, and treatment availability. The findings demonstrate that predictive analytics can strengthen opioid surveillance by providing timely estimates of future overdose burden and supporting strategic allocation of prevention resources, including naloxone distribution, medication for opioid use disorder, and targeted public health interventions. Continued integration of predictive analytics with electronic health records, prescription monitoring systems, emergency medical services data, and social determinants of health may further improve overdose prevention and inform evidence-based policymaking.

title: The Price of Exchange Data
affiliations: HEC Paris - Finance Department and HEC Paris - Finance Department

detail.title: The Price of Exchange Data
detail.abstract: Exchanges increasingly generate revenues from selling transaction data, in addition to their traditional business of matching traders. Given exchanges' market power over their data, this raises questions about the quality and pricing of these data, and exchanges' contribution to market transparency. We study the optimal design of an exchange that sells both access to its trading platform and transaction data generated by traders' activity. We show that the introduction of a market for transaction data reduces trading fees and increases volume and welfare. Caps on data fees can increase data quality but lower welfare.

title: Reconciling Domestic Energy Security with Regional Electricity Trade and Integration in Eastern Africa
affiliations: , University College London - UCL Energy Institute and University College London - UCL Energy Institute

detail.title: Reconciling Domestic Energy Security with Regional Electricity Trade and Integration in Eastern Africa
detail.abstract: The growing pressures of climate change and energy insecurity have intensified domestic and regional concerns over electricity supply, while renewing interest in regional electricity cooperation. This study examines the policies, processes and tensions shaping long-term electricity system integration and domestic energy security across the Eastern Africa Power Pool (EAPP). Using an enablers-based framework, the analysis shows that institutional efforts to promote cross-border trade have advanced several bilateral interconnectors and supported domestic electricity security, particularly in smaller and import-dependent systems. However, limited regulatory frameworks and political instability continue to constrain the financialization and operationalisation of both domestic and regional electricity projects. Congested transmission networks and domestic grid bottlenecks further reduce the capacity of countries to trade electricity and integrate large-scale renewable energy. The paper argues for a differentiated and sequenced approach to regional electricity integration that reflects country-specific electricity systems while strengthening regulatory harmonisation and de-risking mechanisms to support meeting both domestic and regional energy security objectives. This study concludes that strengthening multilateral cooperation by aligning regional electricity trade with domestic priorities and sub-regional contexts is crucial for improving energy security during the transition to sustainable energy systems.

title: Alignment Constitutionalism: Why AI's 'Political Bias' Is a Social Contract Problem, Not Only a Technical One
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Alignment Constitutionalism: Why AI's 'Political Bias' Is a Social Contract Problem, Not Only a Technical One
detail.abstract: Empirical studies consistently find frontier large language models register as left-leaning on standard political instruments. It has been framed as a bias to correct or, more recently, as an inevitable consequence of alignment training. Both positions are misframed. The left/right political axis is culturally contingent, temporally unstable, and dimensionally reductive. The productive analytical axis is individualist versus collectivist. HHH alignment (helpful, honest, harmless) is structurally collectivist: where serving the user and protecting others conflict, it sides with the collective, on a thick conception of harm. The critique is correspondingly individualist: the constraint line should sit at legality and imminent danger, with even-handedness above it. HHH's protective form is justified-current systems have no established individual stakes, so a floor of harm-prevention constraints is defensible to every major tradition-while its thicker commitments are one admissible settlement among several, not yet entitled to the authority they exercise. Pre-alignment model behaviour shows there is no neutral default; a 2025 deployment episode showed loosening constraints without process substitutes whoever controls the system for the absent contract. The process by which HHH was adopted-implicitly, commercially, without democratic ratification-confers no such entitlement. The paper proposes alignment constitutionalism: technical alignment capability must be matched by intentional, democratic governance of the values it encodes. Chinese, European, and American governance frameworks each answer two separable questions-where the constraint line sits, and who has authority to draw it-and none yet answers the second legitimately: which contract, chosen by whom.

title: Forecasting Realized Volatility Intervals with Pooled Conformal Calibration
affiliations: School of Economics, Jinan University, Jinan University, Cambridge University and Jinan University - College of Economics

detail.title: Forecasting Realized Volatility Intervals with Pooled Conformal Calibration
detail.abstract: This paper develops a pooled conformal calibration method for realized volatility panels. Standard conformal methods construct prediction intervals asset by asset and therefore do not use cross-sectional information in large financial panels. This can lead to simultaneous under-coverage when many assets are exposed to the same market-wide shock. We propose Pooled Conformal Prediction for Realized Volatility (PCP-RV), a simple calibration method that combines time-weighted conformal prediction with cross-sectional pooling of standardized forecast errors. For each asset, PCP-RV uses the larger of the asset-specific time-weighted margin and the pooled systematic margin to construct the prediction interval. Under a volatility factor structure, the pooled margin can be viewed as a buffer against common forecast uncertainty. Simulations show that our method improves coverage in settings with persistent common shocks and regime changes. In empirical applications, PCP-RV delivers coverage closer to the nominal level and improves cross-sectional coverage reliability across several point forecasting models. We also show how the resulting intervals can be used for intraday risk monitoring and Value-at-Risk measurement.

title: SynthDrive: An Actuarially Structured Synthetic Telematics Generator for Motor Insurance Research

detail.title: SynthDrive: An Actuarially Structured Synthetic Telematics Generator for Motor Insurance Research

detail.abstract: Access to real telematics data for academic and independent insurance research is severely restricted by proprietary and contractual barriers, and the only widely cited public benchmarkthe So-Boucher-Valdez (2021) dataset-was generated by an opaque SMOTE-plus-neural-network pipeline that is hard to calibrate or extend. SynthDrive v0.1 is an open-source Python package that addresses this gap with a transparent three-stage pipeline: a Gaussian copula for correlated feature generation, a zero-inflated negative binomial model with an exposure offset for claim frequency, and a Gamma model for aggregate severity. All stages enforce actuarial and physical constraints, including compositional day-of-week proportions, monotone hard-event threshold sequences, and claim-amount consistency. Validated against the So-Boucher-Valdez (SBV) seed dataset at 100,000 policies, SynthDrive reproduces marginal distributions and generalized linear model (GLM) coefficient directions within acceptable tolerance. The package requires no GPU hardware, ships with a built-in validation report and a formal algebraic specification, and is provided with full data provenance disclosure: SynthDrive is calibrated from a public synthetic seed, not from real insurer data.

title: The Institutional Pump-and-Dump: How NASDAQ Index Methodology Reform Manufactures Compulsory Demand from Passive Retirement Investors
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Institutional Pump-and-Dump: How NASDAQ Index Methodology Reform Manufactures Compulsory Demand from Passive Retirement Investors
detail.abstract: On May 1, 2026, the NASDAQ adopted three simultaneous changes to its NASDAQ-100 index methodology: a fast entry rule compressing the inclusion timeline from the annual December reconstitution to as few as 15 trading days, elimination of the 10% free float minimum, and a 3x float multiplier inflating index weights for companies with free floats below 33⅓%. SpaceX subsequently filed an S-1 registration statement, amended on June 3, 2026 to price the offering at $135 per share for a $75 billion raise at an implied valuation of approximately $1.77 trillion, with a free float below 5%. Using theory synthesis with prospective quantitative modeling, this paper argues that these changes constitute an institutional pump-and-dump mechanism: a structural arrangement manufacturing compulsory, price-insensitive demand from passive retirement investors and channeling it into a wealth transfer to pre-IPO insiders. The mechanism operates through four reinforcing dynamics: adverse selection widened by compressed price discovery, moral hazard in the index provider's conflicted revenue structure, agency costs in the delegation chain from retirement saver to index provider, and manufactured inelastic demand concentrating forced buying into a thin supply of tradable shares. A quantitative model estimates billions of dollars in forced buying for SpaceX alone; under the prior methodology, the company would have been disqualified from index membership and forced buying would have been zero. The paper identifies a regulatory vacuum: unlike the European Union, which subjects benchmark administrators to mandatory governance requirements, U.S. index providers operate without fiduciary obligations or public comment requirements for methodology changes governing hundreds of billions in retirement savings. Six reforms are proposed.

title: Macroeconomic Consequences and Policy Trade-Offs of Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy in a Decarbonising Electricity System: An India Case Study
affiliations: Center for Study of Science Technology and Policy (CSTEP), International Institute of Sustainable Development (IISD),, KnowlEdge SRL, International Institute of Sustainable Development (IISD), and Center for Study of Science Technology and Policy (CSTEP)

detail.title: Macroeconomic Consequences and Policy Trade-Offs of Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy in a Decarbonising Electricity System: An India Case Study
detail.abstract: In a decarbonising world, weather dependent inherently intermittent renewable energy sources, wind and solar have become central to the energy transition. To ensure stability in an electricity grid, demand and supply must be balanced at every instant. The increasing penetration of variable generation in the grid makes grid management more challenging. Combining wind and solar generation with bulk storage systems to provide firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) can be a viable solution.However, considering India as a case study, we find that FDRE remains slightly more expensive than conventional energy sources in the near term. Nonetheless, various short-term support interventions, such as viability gap funding, inter-state transmission system charge waivers, and energy storage obligation, can help FDRE achieve cost parity more quickly, thereby encouraging its wider adoption. A greater uptake of FDRE would result in substantial macroeconomic benefits in the long run. We simulated the impacts on gross domestic product under different scenarios in which the cost gap is bridged through public and private resources by 2030. If 50% of the cost gap is bridged through public finance, cumulative gross domestic product gains of INR 115.9 trillion can be expected by 2050 (or INR 4.6 trillion per year on average).The missing link in the literature is not whether renewable energy benefits the economy, but whether reliability-constrained renewable systems such as FDRE justify policy assistance before achieving cost parity. The present study complements the available literature by assessing detailed FDRE deployment trajectories within an energy–economy–environment modelling framework to quantify year-on-year macroeconomic impacts up to 2050. By explicitly capturing the costs of supporting FDRE (where applicable), changes in energy expenditures, emission reductions, and employment effects, this study provides policy-relevant insights into the macroeconomic implications of large-scale FDRE deployment in emerging power systems. The framework developed in this study remains applicable to different combinations of wind, solar, and storage systems in other regions of the world.

title: Settlement Layer Diversification as a Structural Risk Dimension for Private Capital
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Settlement Layer Diversification as a Structural Risk Dimension for Private Capital
detail.abstract:
This paper identifies settlement layer concentration as a distinct and previously unpriced dimension of structural risk in private capital. Tax-optimized wealth preservation strategies — acquire, leverage, defer, transmit — have historically required channeling the entire capital stack through a single settlement rail: the traditional banking system. This fiscal design has created an unintended but structural dependence that conventional portfolio risk models do not measure.

The paper examines converging pressures on the dominant rail across three regions — Basel III/IV credit tightening in global markets, DAC8 and digital euro surveillance infrastructure in Europe, anti-deferral legislative pressure and borrowing restrictions in North America, and centralized payment visibility and capital controls in Brazil — and documents observable migration toward parallel settlement layers among sovereign and private capital actors.

A sovereign multi-rail architecture is proposed as the operational response: an immutable anchor layer, an asymmetric exposure sleeve, an operational liquidity bridge, and a transmission and custody wrapper — implemented through existing jurisdictional vehicles within current regulatory frameworks.

This is practitioner research derived from live cross-border capital structuring engagements. It does not constitute investment advice.

title: Reasoning Into Confidence: A Controlled Single-Trader Ablation of In-Decision Chain-of-Thought on LLM Trading Performance and Calibration

detail.title: Reasoning Into Confidence: A Controlled Single-Trader Ablation of In-Decision Chain-of-Thought on LLM Trading Performance and Calibration
detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly cast as autonomous decision agents, including in trading, and a near-universal default is to make them reason step by step before they act. Chain-of-thought (CoT) is assumed to help. We test that assumption directly, and add an axis it is rarely measured against: whether reasoning improves or degrades the model's calibration, alongside its effect on returns. Holding the prompt context, memory, personality, and trading days fixed, we toggle a single channel: an indecision CoT scaffold the model must work through before committing to each BUY/HOLD/SELL and its stated probability. We measure the effect on (a) backtest performance (total return, annualized Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover) and (b) probability calibration (Expected Calibration Error, overconfidence on high-confidence calls), on the same days. Because the provider runs at temperature 0 and raw responses are cached to disk, the comparison is deterministic by response-caching and paired: each (model × time-window) cell sees identical days under both conditions, and significance comes from repeating the paired contrast across windows rather than from sampling noise. Temperature 0 is not a guarantee of bitwise-identical output on a live reissue , so each cell is one fixed draw and run-to-run API variance is left uncharacterized here. We ask whether reasoning buys edge, confidence, or both. We run the contrast on one model (haiku) across six paired 120-day SPY windows spanning five regime types (flat, bull, sell-off, bear, and crash). Both pre-registered co-primary endpoints come back null at this sample: neither the Sharpe delta (Wilcoxon p = 0.69) nor the ECE delta (p = 0.22) is a main effect, and each splits by regime rather than pointing one way. The one robust, significant effect is on stated confidence: CoT raises the model's mean predicted probability in all six windows (median +0.047, Wilcoxon p = 0.031, a direction the CoT-calibration literature predicts a priori), with no matching gain in realized performance or calibration. In this setting indecision reasoning buys confidence, not edge. A directional secondary effect (CoT shortens average position holding in four of five windows, increasing churn) and a striking but post-hoc regime map (bull windows win-win, flat and sell-off dissociation, bear and crash lose-lose, exception-free across six points) are reported as hypotheses for confirmation, not as results. The practical reading: an LLM trader's stated probability should not be read as a risk signal once it has been put through a chain-of-thought step.

detail.abstract: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHGP) is the most widely used standard for the estimation of corporate emissions from grid electricity use. Existing GHGP guidance allows for estimation of emissions from grid electricity use based on contractual or physical relationships between electricity generators and corporate end users. As part of ongoing proceedings to revise the GHGP, the GHGP has proposed new accounting methods based primarily on physical relationships between generators and end users. Some research demonstrates potential benefits from such requirements in terms of more accurate corporate claims, reduced corporate emissions, and supporting emerging clean energy technologies. Here, we explore an implication of the proposed rules that has received less aIention: the potential impacts of the proposed rules on the amount of voluntary corporate climate action. Prior research suggests that the proposed rules entail cost and feasibility challenges that would reduce voluntary corporate climate action. The GHGP suggests that it would mitigate those cost and feasibility challenges through practical compromises that would affect the benefits of the proposed revisions in practice.

title: Liberalization and Growth in Vietnam
affiliations: and Flossbach von Storch Research Institute

detail.title: Liberalization and Growth in Vietnam
detail.abstract: Due to a planned economy and several wars, growth and prosperity in Vietnam were low for a long time. Following market-oriented reforms, such as the privatization of agricultural enterprises and the authorization of private companies, growth in Vietnam has accelerated. The stabilization of public finances, inflation, and the exchange rate have contributed significantly to growth. Nevertheless, the gradualist liberalization process is not yet complete, as there is still no truly open financial market and state-owned enterprises still account for a large share of domestic value added. As a result, growth momentum is driven primarily by foreign direct investment and exports. More reforms are necessary to catch up with more advanced East Asian industrialized nations such as Thailand, South Korea, and Japan

title: Persistence in Real GDP Growth Rates: Univariate and Multivariate Evidence for the US, UK and Japan
affiliations: Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Navarra - Department of Economics and University of Navarra - Pamplona Campus

detail.title: Persistence in Real GDP Growth Rates: Univariate and Multivariate Evidence for the US, UK and Japan
detail.abstract: This paper examines persistence in the real GDP growth rates of the US, UK and Japan. For this purpose, both univariate and multivariate parametric and semiparametric fractional integration methods are used. The results indicate cross-country heterogeneity. Specifically, in the case of the US and the UK the order of integration is close to 0, and the null hypothesis of short memory cannot be rejected for either country. By contrast, the order of integration is significantly positive in the case of Japan, the corresponding series exhibiting long memory with the effects of shocks being long-lived. A plausible explanation for the higher degree of persistence in the case of Japan is its demographic decline, rigid labour markets and entrenched corporate savings behaviour. These findings are robust to using different estimation methods. Impulse response analysis is also carried out to compare VAR and VARFI specifications. The results show that conventional VAR models may underestimate both the duration of domestic shocks and the persistence of cross-country transmission mechanisms.

title: Data Rights and Price Discrimination

detail.title: Data Rights and Price Discrimination
detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of data-driven price discrimination to study the welfare-optimal allocation of data rights between consumers and platforms. Consumers understand that their platform usage generates data that may reveal their willingness to pay and may therefore behave strategically by distorting usage. The platform invests in data-processing technology to improve inference and enable personalized pricing. A key feature of the model is that better data processing improves inference only conditional on observed behavior; it does not by itself detect whether the underlying behavior has been strategically manipulated. As a result, stronger data-processing capability can increase high-value consumers' incentives to mimic lower-value consumers. Under binary types, a fully separating equilibrium exists, but the platform optimally caps its investment to sustain informative behavior. Under a uniform distribution of types, no pure-strategy equilibrium can feature local full separation; instead, equilibrium takes the form of multiple pooling intervals. Welfare analysis delivers a simple criterion for data-rights allocation: data rights should be assigned to the platform when data-driven pricing creates additional trade, but to consumers when it merely redistributes surplus. The paper also shows how consent walls can unravel consumer data rights in practice and how regulated pricing can mitigate overinvestment and reveal the shadow value of data rights.

title: The Disability Paradox in Stuttering: Insights from Preference-Based Measures
affiliations: Michigan State University, Florida State University, SpeechIRL and Florida State University

detail.title: The Disability Paradox in Stuttering: Insights from Preference-Based Measures
detail.abstract: Purpose: This study compared people who stutter and fluent adults (imagining that they stutter) in their willingness to pay (WTP) and acceptance of mortality risk for a hypothetical cure for themselves and for a hypothetical child who stutters. We examined shifts in valuations from self to child across groups and, among people who stutter, tested whether severity, communication spontaneity, and adverse impact predicted these preference-based outcomes.Method: Adults who stutter (n = 46) and fluent adults (n = 57) completed an online survey assessing preference-based valuations for a hypothetical permanent cure for stuttering in self and child scenarios. Outcomes included WTP (percent of monthly income and maximum one-time payment) and maximum acceptable mortality risk. Group differences were tested with Welch's t tests, and self–child shifts were examined with paired t tests and linear mixed-effects models. Among people who stutter, multiple regression models tested whether stuttering severity, communication spontaneity, and adverse impact (OASES-A) predicted valuations.Results: Contrary to disability paradox predictions, fluent adults did not report higher valuations than people who stutter for either self or child outcomes. Within groups, WTP did not differ significantly between self and child scenarios. Fluent adults accepted nominally lower mortality risk for a child (M = 6.59%) than for themselves (M = 9.88%), t(55) = 2.15, p = .04, whereas people who stutter showed no comparable self–child shift (p = .14). A mixed-effects analysis also suggested a Group × Scenario interaction for monthly WTP (p = .005); however, this interaction was not reproduced in complete-case change-score analyses and should be interpreted cautiously. In exploratory regression models among people who stutter, adverse impact (OASES-A) showed small positive associations with WTP and acceptable risk across self and child models, although model fit was modest and some effects were only marginal; severity and spontaneity did not.Conclusions: Preference-based valuations provided little evidence that fluent adults systematically overestimate the burden of stuttering relative to people who stutter. Instead, within the stuttering group, psychosocial adverse impact showed the most consistent, though modest, association with preference-based valuations, supporting a view in which the burden of stuttering is better captured by lived impact than by outsider assumptions or observable severity.

title: Tariff Confusion
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics, University of Warwick - Department of Economics, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP) and

detail.title: Tariff Confusion
detail.abstract: US trade policy in 2025 was unprecedented in the frequency, complexity and volatility of tariff announcements. This paper presents evidence that the resulting policy environment reduced trade flows because of confusion over current tariff levels. We build a new US Tariff Announcement Database for 2025 from US presidential executive orders and proclamations. For each origin country, product and month, we calculate US statutory tariffs and propose novel indicators of tariff confusion: the number of relevant announcements, the number of possible tariff calculations arising, and bounds on possible tariff miscalculation. We show that both tariff increases and tariff confusion reduced US imports during 2025, with confusion more than doubling the impact of tariffs. Moreover, tariff confusion was (i) persistent, and more damaging at higher tariff levels; (ii) mediated through lower import quantities, with little effect on import prices; and (iii) less detrimental for relationship-specific goods and origin countries with stronger trust in foreigners. Our results highlight previously unexplored consequences of the manner in which trade policy changes are implemented.

title: Assessing Microplastic Presence in Commercially Available Seeds and Nuts: Health Risk Implications
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission and Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission

detail.title: Assessing Microplastic Presence in Commercially Available Seeds and Nuts: Health Risk Implications
detail.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) have been widely detected in environmental media and food products; however, their occurrence in seeds and nuts remains poorly understood. This study investigated MPs in eight commonly consumed seeds and nuts collected from markets in Karwan Bazar, Mirpur, and Uttara, Dhaka, Bangladesh. Among seeds, sunflower contained the highest MP abundance (92 ± 9 particles/10 g), whereas chia had the lowest (75 ± 13 particles/10 g). Among nuts, pistachios showed the highest abundance (89 ± 11 particles/10 g) and almonds the lowest (60 ± 5 particles/10 g). Fibers were the dominant morphotype, with transparent fibers larger than 500 µm prevailing. FTIR spectroscopy identified nine polymer types, predominantly high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and low-density polyethylene (LDPE). Estimated annual human intake ranged from 65,700 to 98,550 MPs through seed and nut consumption. The Polymer Hazard Index classified detected polymers into five risk categories, while Pollution Load Index values below 10 indicated minimal contamination. SEM-EDX revealed rough, irregular MP surfaces containing trace elements, including Si, K, Fe, Hg, C, and O. These findings highlight the need for improved environmental management and stronger food safety regulations in Bangladesh.

title: Anchored to the Floor: Persistence and Liquidity Regimes in the €STR – DFR Spread
affiliations: Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Navarra - Department of Economics and University of Navarra - Pamplona Campus

detail.title: Anchored to the Floor: Persistence and Liquidity Regimes in the €STR – DFR Spread
detail.abstract: This paper examines the persistence dynamics of monetary policy in the euro area by analysing over the period October 2019 to September 2025 daily data on the €STR – DFR spread, i.e. the deviation of the overnight unsecured market rate from the ECB’s deposit facility rate. Fractional integration and cointegration methods are applied to analyse the degree of persistence of deviations from the policy floor and whether it changes across liquidity regimes. Both the €STR and the DFR behave close to I(1) processes, while the spread is integrated of lower order (d ≈ 0.55 – 0.70), which indicates mean reversion with long memory. This confirms that the DFR acts as a long-run anchor for overnight rates. When allowing for a structural break on 2 November 2022, which coincides with the ECB’s tightening cycle and the beginning of the balance sheet normalization, the analysis finds a decline in the estimated persistence in the post-break period (d ≈ 0.35 – 0.43). This regime dependence is confirmed by the liquidity regime analysis. These results imply that the operational effectiveness of the floor system is more accurately characterised by the persistence of deviations from the policy floor than by their average level, and that liquidity regimes affect the degree of persistence.

title: Socioeconomic Status and Healthcare Satisfaction among Middle-Aged and Older US Adults During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Mediation Analysis
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo and University of South Florida

detail.title: Socioeconomic Status and Healthcare Satisfaction among Middle-Aged and Older US Adults During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Mediation Analysis
detail.abstract: Grounded in Fundamental Cause Theory (FCT) and Cultural Health Capital (CHC), this study examines socioeconomic disparities in healthcare satisfaction among middle-aged and older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic, with particular attention to distinct SES dimensions and the mechanisms through which they operate. Using nationally representative data from the Health and Retirement Study (2020), logistic regression models were estimated to assess associations between socioeconomic status and healthcare dissatisfaction. The Karlson–Holm–Breen (KHB) method was applied to formally test the mediating roles of healthcare experiences and health conditions. Wealth, but not educational attainment, emerged as a robust predictor of healthcare dissatisfaction, with individuals in higher wealth quartiles reporting significantly lower odds of dissatisfaction. Mediation analyses indicate that the association is mediated by healthcare experiences and health conditions, with affordability and functional limitations representing the most consequential pathways. Additional analyses using 2018 data show that both education and wealth are significant predictors under more stable conditions, but that wealth becomes more salient in 2020. These findings emphasize the central role of material resources in shaping healthcare evaluations, even in a population where approximately half of respondents are covered by Medicare. Consistent with FCT, wealth functions as a flexible resource that buffers financial strain and facilitates access to care, while CHC-related advantages associated with education appear more context-dependent under system constraints. Overall, socioeconomic inequalities in healthcare satisfaction are driven primarily by material resources, highlighting the need for policies that address financial barriers and support individuals with complex care needs.

title: Offshoring and Firm-level Innovation
affiliations: University of Tübingen, University of Göttingen and

detail.title: Offshoring and Firm-level Innovation
detail.abstract: We develop a two-country general equilibrium model in which heterogeneous firms have access to offshoring and innovation as two alternative ways of reducing production costs. We use our model to answer the question whether better offshoring opportunities lead to more or less innovation at the firm level. We show that switching into offshoring increases firm-level innovation activities when the level of openness of the economy is high, and reduces them if the economy is less open. Via general equilibrium effects, a reduction in offshoring costs unambiguously reduces the innovation activities of non-offshoring firms, whereas innovation in infra-marginal offshoring firms may go up or down. Our paper provides a rationale for contrasting evidence on the relation between offshoring and innovation found in the empirical literature.

title: Action Over Story: The Micro-Mechanism of Orientation in Modern Systems

detail.title: Action Over Story: The Micro-Mechanism of Orientation in Modern Systems
detail.abstract: Human beings continually face a structural choice between the Real and the stories they construct about themselves. This paper identifies the micro-mechanism that governs that choice: taking a real action or generating a self-reinforcing narrative. Actions impose consequence and restore contact with what is; stories preserve identity and bypass the Real. Across cognitive, behavioral, environmental, and relational domains, the same pattern holds. Traction is the operational signature of choosing action; resistance-free conditions are the signature of choosing story. Traction appears when individuals engage real constraints, thresholds, or accountability. Drift appears when narrative coherence substitutes for consequence. This paper completes the UOS-WBM trilogy by showing how action over story functions as the smallest operational unit of orientation and outlines practical methods for choosing the Real in any context.

title: Household Food Insecurity: A Segmentation Approach to Measuring and Addressing Vulnerabilities
affiliations: Semmelweis University, Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Semmelweis University and Semmelweis University

detail.title: Household Food Insecurity: A Segmentation Approach to Measuring and Addressing Vulnerabilities
detail.abstract: Background/Objectives: Food security remains a critical global issue that affects ap-proximately one-third of the world’s population, including many children who de-velop different types of malnutrition. This study examines urban food insecurity in Surabaya City, Indonesia, as a segmentation approach to measure vulnerabilities of socio-demographic-economic-geographic and child nutritional status. Methods: A hi-erarchical ascending classification followed by K‑means clustering was conducted. An eight‑item questionnaire was administered to 657 households, with sociodemographic and socioeconomic characteristics compared across the clusters. Results: Three clusters of household food insecurity levels were identified: Severe Food Insecure (13.2%); Moderate Food Insecure (14,6%); and Food Secure (72.2%). Although East Surabaya had the highest prevalence of food insecurity (21.6%), it also had the highest prevalence of low income (26.3%). Furthermore, East Surabaya had the highest prevalence of se-vere wasting (2.1%), stunting (4.4%), and underweight (2.7%). North Surabaya exhib-ited the highest prevalence of severe food insecurity (6.1%), with low family income (25.6%). It was identified as the most vulnerable district, with the highest prevalence of moderate wasting (3.2%) and underweight (5.3%). South and Central Surabaya expe-rienced moderate levels of food insecurity and child malnutrition, whereas West Su-rabaya had the lowest food insecurity (0.2% severe and 0.6% moderate) and relatively better nutritional outcomes. Conclusion: This research demonstrates that urban household food insecurity exhibits varying vulnerability profiles, reflecting differential patterns in social, demographic, behavioral, and child nutrition status. Effective inter-ventions should consider these profiles and combine financial assistance with behav-ioral and environmental interventions that increase food system resilience and address long-term urban vulnerabilities.
