detail.abstract:
"The consequences of failing to solve the great dilemma of risk won't just appear as abstract figures in the newspaper. They are all too real-people's savings wiped out, governments forced to tax or inflate their economies to death-human tragedy with real economic consequences. This is not my opinion. It is just simple math."
                                                                        -Mark Spitznagel, Safe Haven: Investing for Financial Storms (2021).

I think we've spent half a century demonizing volatility as "randomness" and, in doing so, invented modern finance rather than truly quantifying financial markets. Simplification has its place—mathematically, linear approximations often work beautifully—but in finance, I believe we went further: we denied our own reality.

I'm not here to argue whether markets are efficient or whether dividends and discounted cash flow models are the holy grail of valuation. I'm here to remind readers of the severity of the quote above. We can debate theory endlessly in a classroom, but when it comes to real people's capital—real lives—as fiduciaries, there is no excuse for negligence. There should also be no excuse for how we educate the next generation of finance students who, despite the industry's growing preference for the quantitatively adept, may one day find themselves responsible for someone else's financial future.

Long gone are the days of discretionary stock-picking on the buy-side. The modern fiduciary standard, regulatory environment, and sheer availability of data demand quantitative justification. But don't worry—this paper is not a critique of Modern Portfolio Theory, nor is it a treatise on non-zero quadratic variation, nonlinearity, or stochastic processes.

Rather, through the lens of a capstone project (shoutout Dr. Neumann), we have an opportunity to revisit some of the most fundamental questions in asset selection and portfolio construction. Augmented by both academic study and industry experience in computational finance, this paper serves as a brief but careful exploration of what it actually means to select equities responsibly in 2025.

Ironically, as you'll see, we often arrive at many of the same conclusions a classical analyst might reach. The difference is not necessarily what we choose, but how we arrive there: independently, quantitatively, and with every assumption exposed to scrutiny.

After all, investing was never about finding gold hidden beneath the surface. It was about learning how to search for it. The real treasure isn't the gold—it's the hunt.

title: Monetary Tightening and the Coal Margin: Evidence from the US Electricity Sector

detail.title: Monetary Tightening and the Coal Margin: Evidence from the US Electricity Sector
detail.abstract: Does unexpected monetary tightening change the fuel composition of electricity generation? This paper studies this question by using high-frequency monetary policy surprises from Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. It uses monthly U.S. state-level electricity data from 2005 to 2023 with predetermined fossil-capacity exposure. The empirical design compares how states with different pre-2005 fossil-capacity exposure respond to the same national monetary policy surprise, while absorbing state-specific seasonality and Census-division-by-year-month shocks. The main result is that contractionary monetary policy surprises reduce coal generation share more strongly in states with higher pre-existing fossil-capacity exposure. For a state at the 75th percentile of pre period fossil capacity exposure relative to one at the 25th percentile, a one standard deviation tightening surprise lowers the coal generation share by 0.117 percentage points. This is equivalent to a coal share reallocation of about 7,834 MWh at average monthly state generation. The result is strongest for coal, survives leave-one-state-out, and exposurerandomization checks, and is not driven by a sustained anticipatory trend. Mechanism evidence shows that coal loses share while natural gas gains share, including within fossil generation itself. The findings point to a short-run fuel-composition channel of monetary policy transmission in which coal is the central adjustment margin in fossil-capacity dependent electricity systems.

title: Grassmannian and SPD Geometry of Dynamic Factor Covariance Models
affiliations: CUNY Baruch College and

detail.title: Grassmannian and SPD Geometry of Dynamic Factor Covariance Models
detail.abstract:
We develop a geometric framework for analyzing dynamic factor covariance models in portfolio management. A low-rank systematic covariance matrix admits the representation 

                          Σsys = UAU⊤,  U ∈St(k,N),  A∈SPD(k),  

with the equivalence relation
                           (U, A) ∼ (UQ, Q⊤AQ),  Q∈O(k). Thus the geometry of a rank-k covariance matrix naturally separates into two coupled components: the Grassmannian geometry of the support subspace [U] ∈ Gr(k,N), and the symmetric positive-definite (SPD) geometry of the covariance structure within that subspace. In dynamic factor models, this leads to two geometric processes, 
                           t → [Ut] ∈ Gr(k,N),   t → At ∈ SPD(k). 

We argue that these processes provide complementary diagnostics for portfolio models. Grassmannian statistics measure the motion, stability, and regime variation of systematic return directions, while SPD statistics measure within-factor risk concentration, conditioning, and covariance deformation. This separation distinguishes models whose apparent complexity arises from moving factor directions from models whose complexity arises from changing risk geometry within a stable factor span. The framework connects fixed-rank positive semidefinite (PSD) geometry, conditional factor models such as instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) and its macro-conditioned variant (GIPCA), and practical diagnostics for covariance forecasting, portfolio turnover, and risk management.

title: Cross-Context Human–Robot Trust Recognition via Multimodal Physiological Fusion for Intelligent Construction
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology and Umeå University

detail.title: Cross-Context Human–Robot Trust Recognition via Multimodal Physiological Fusion for Intelligent Construction
detail.abstract: Trust recognition is essential for ensuring safe and effective human–robot collaboration (HRC) in intelligent construction. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has been widely adopted for trust recognition, its performance often deteriorates across different contexts because dynamic tasks and environmental disturbances alter the EEG feature distributions. To address this challenge, this study proposes a cross-context trust recognition framework that integrates EEG with electrodermal activity (EDA), electrocardiography (ECG), and photoplethysmography (PPG). The framework was validated through three experiments encompassing static, virtual, and real-world HRC scenarios. The results show that, under cross-context transfer, the multimodal model achieves an MAE of 5.81, an R² of 0.61, and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.79, outperforming the EEG-only baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate that EDA, ECG, and PPG provide complementary trust-related information, improving prediction accuracy, robustness, and generalization capability. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of multimodal physiological signal fusion for reliable trust recognition across diverse construction contexts.

title: Internal Cooling Tube Geometry with Integrated Leds Affects Light Distribution and Chlorella Vulgaris Growth
affiliations: Sanmenxia Foreign Language Senior High School

detail.title: Internal Cooling Tube Geometry with Integrated Leds Affects Light Distribution and Chlorella Vulgaris Growth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethical approval was required for this study. Chlorella vulgaris (strain FACHB-8) is a non-pathogenic, GRAS-listed microalga commonly used in laboratory research. The study did not involve human subjects, vertebrate animals, or genetically modified organisms.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The equipment used in this study (spectrophotometer, analytical balance, thermostatic water bath, magnetic stirrers) was provided by the chemistry laboratory of Sanmenxia Foreign Language Senior High School.

detail.abstract:
Background: Temperature control remains a bottleneck in bench-scale photobioreactor (PBR) operation. Internal cooling tubes improve heat removal but inevitably obstruct light. Winding LED strips directly around cooling tubes-co-locating the light source and heat exchangermay mitigate this trade-off, but the effect of tube geometry on the resulting light field has not been experimentally quantified. 

Methods: Three internal cooling-tube geometries (serpentine coil, vertical straight tube, horizontal straight tube), each fabricated from identical borosilicate glass (OD 8 mm, length 900 mm) and fitted with identical flexible LED strips (660 + 450 nm), were compared against a notube control in 1.5-L batch cultures of Chlorella vulgaris (n = 3 per treatment, 12 beakers total). Spatial PAR distribution (5 × 5 grid, 25 positions per beaker), temperature at three depths, biomass (OD₇₅₀/CDW), chlorophyll content, and pH were monitored over 12 days. Data were analysed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD post-hoc tests (α = 0.05) using R 4.3.1. 

Results: The serpentine coil provided the most uniform temperature control (intra-beaker spatial range 0.5 ± 0.2 °C vs. 1.1 ± 0.3 °C for vertical and 1.6 ± 0.4 °C for horizontal tubes). Net PAR obstruction was 8.2 ± 2.9% (serpentine), 7.5 ± 2.6% (vertical), and 14.1 ± 3.2% (horizontal; P = 0.012 vs. serpentine). Despite these differences, final biomass (1.69-1.82 g L⁻¹) and specific growth rate (0.36-0.43 d⁻¹) did not differ significantly among the cooled configurations (P = 0.18-0.52), consistent with operation above the light-saturation threshold of C. vulgaris. 

Conclusions: Under the tested conditions (~120 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹), tube geometry measurably affects light distribution and temperature uniformity but not growth. The serpentine coil with integrated LED lighting offers the best combination of thermal performance and apparatus simplicity for bench-scale experiments where temperature-sensitive endpoints are of interest.

title: Trickle-down Belief, Institutional Skepticism, and the Governance Imperative in Namibia's Emerging Petroleum Sector Policy Article -oil and Gas Transportation Governance

detail.title: Trickle-down Belief, Institutional Skepticism, and the Governance Imperative in Namibia's Emerging Petroleum Sector Policy Article -oil and Gas Transportation Governance

declarations.ethicsApproval: ethic commirr ethics committee aproved

detail.abstract:
Namibia stands at a crossroads that few African states have navigated well. Offshore oil and gas reserves of potential
generational magnitude are edging toward commercial exploitation — and with them comes a governance challenge
that is simultaneously technical, institutional, and political. This article examines a paradox surfaced by a survey of
seventeen oil and gas transportation industry stakeholders: near-universal belief that infrastructure investment will yield
transformative economic benefits sits uneasily beside deep scepticism about whether current government policy
frameworks can actually deliver those benefits to ordinary Namibians.
The headline findings are stark. Ninety-four point one percent of respondents expect significant direct employment
from oil and gas transportation infrastructure. Eighty-two point four percent believe ancillary local businesses will
emerge and grow. Yet only 52.9% have confidence that current government initiatives are adequate to ensure equitable
distribution of those benefits — and 23.5% actively disagree with that adequacy claim. Seventy-six point five percent
support a dedicated local capacity development fund, a preference that persists even among those nominally satisfied
with existing policy, revealing a structural demand for institutional reinforcement that rhetoric alone will not satisfy.
The article situates these findings within comparative petroleum governance literature — drawing on Ghana, Angola,
Norway, Trinidad and Tobago, Brazil, and Kazakhstan — to distil lessons that are analytically applicable to the
Namibian context. It identifies four priority reform axes: diagnostic precision on the sources of the confidence deficit;
transparency and accountability architecture that makes benefit flows visible and verifiable; phased local content
progression calibrated to realistic capability timelines; and hybrid governance for any dedicated fund. The
recommendations are direct: Namibia has a narrow window to design governance frameworks that convert optimism
into durable, equitably distributed economic gains. History offers no shortage of cautionary precedents. The choice is
whether to learn from them.

title: International Sanctions and Constitutional Compliance
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Institute of Law and Economics, University of Trier - Faculty of Economics and University of Trier - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: International Sanctions and Constitutional Compliance
detail.abstract: Many studies have evaluated whether sanctions improve or harm the living conditions of target populations, for example in terms of the protection of human rights. However, judging governments' responses to international sanctions based on their compliance with a universal human rights standard has been criticized as an imposition of Western values. We propose an alternative benchmark for government action that is not subject to the same criticism: whether governments comply with their own national constitutions as codified forms of the national social contract. Our analysis of 182 countries over the period 1962 to 2022 using panel DiD and event study estimators corroborates our theoretical expectation that government responses depend on the target's regime type. Whereas democracies improve their constitutional compliance under sanction pressure, autocracies start complying even less. These results suggest that sanctions can only make governments comply with their legal commitments if those governments face binding reelection constraints.

title: Explainable Identification of Radiomic Features for Diffuse Interstitial Lung Disease Patterns in CT Images
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Explainable Identification of Radiomic Features for Diffuse Interstitial Lung Disease Patterns in CT Images
detail.abstract: Diffuse Interstitial Lung Diseases (DILD) present significant challenges for radiological diagnosis due to the subtle visual differences between radiological patterns in computed tomography (CT) images and the reliance on physician expertise. This study proposes a methodology to identify the most relevant features associated with DILD radiological patterns using explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including decision trees and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), to enhance model transparency and interpretability. Radiomic features, including first- and second-order statistical descriptors, were extracted from regions of interest, with second-order texture features derived from the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM). These features were used to train and evaluate several machine learning classification models. Among the evaluated models, the artificial neural network achieved the best performance, reaching an overall accuracy of 91.84% and F1-scores up to 96.32% for specific radiological patterns. The analysis allowed the identification of the most relevant features associated with each radiological pattern (ground-glass, consolidation, micronodules, and healthy tissue). First-order features, particularly the median and mean, consistently appeared among the most significant attributes across patterns, while second-order GLCM features contributed strongly to the classification of more complex patterns. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach can effectively identify key features of DILD patterns in CT images, supporting the development of interpretable computer-aided diagnostic tools for radiological analysis.

title: Determinants of Greenhouse Gas Emissions in South Asia: Panel Evidence from an Environmental Kuznets Curve Framework

detail.title: Determinants of Greenhouse Gas Emissions in South Asia: Panel Evidence from an Environmental Kuznets Curve Framework
detail.abstract: This paper examines the determinants of greenhouse gas emissions of south Asian countries Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka from 1990-2023 by following an EKC model. CIPS shows the mixed I (0)/I (1) integration order suitable for panel ARDL framework. Pooled Mean Group (PMG) estimator is preferred over Dynamic Fixed Effects by the Hausman test and cross-validated using DOLS and FMOLS. PMG and DOLS both indicate a U-shaped relationship between income and emissions, the opposite of the traditional inverted-U EKC. Energy consumption is most consistent driver for all three estimators, in the long-run. The correlation between trade openness and emissions is positive and consistent with the pollution haven hypothesis, whereas the effects of FDI on emissions are uniformly found to be insignificant, and the effect of urbanization on emissions is different by country and by estimator. The pooled error correction term is negative and statistically significant, indicating that it is a long-run attractor and that the adjustment rate is around 45% per year. Growth in GHG emissions in South Asia do not happen automatically under the EKC self-correction mechanism. Decarbonization and green trade policy action is needed to meet Paris agreement commitments.

title: Nearshoring Under Binding Infrastructure Constraints and Financial Frictions: A Microfounded Agent-Based Model for Mexico
affiliations: Universidad de Antioquia and Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico

detail.title: Nearshoring Under Binding Infrastructure Constraints and Financial Frictions: A Microfounded Agent-Based Model for Mexico
detail.abstract: Mexico’s nearshoring window—propelled by US–China decoupling and the USMCA—faces binding constraints: weak private investment, overstretched electricity grids, and water stress in key manufacturing corridors (The Economist, 2026; DP World and Economist Impact, 2025). We develop a microfounded agent-based model calibrated with Mexican state-level panel data (32 states, 2017–2024) that integrates Melitz heterogeneous-firm trade theory, Krugman new economic geography, and Handley–Limaõ trade-policy uncertainty. Parameters follow a three-box provenance taxonomy: estimated from our own panel via stochastic frontier analysis and double/debiased machine learning, taken from peer-reviewed literature, or calibrated via ABC-SMC with Morris sensitivity screening. The calibrated model reproduces six of nine target moments within 15%. Nine counterfactual experiments identify optimal infrastructure allocation (+10%) and targeted infrastructure investment (+8%) as the interventions with the largest expected export gains; wide confidence intervals across seeds reflect genuine heterogeneity in regional responses. Forward projections to 2031 yield economically plausible trajectories, with a policy bundle adding +3.7% to national manufacturing exports.

title: A Riemann Thorin-van Dantzig principle
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: A Riemann Thorin-van Dantzig principle
detail.abstract: Two probabilistic programmes attack the location of zeros of an even entire function: the van Dantzig-Lukacs programme, which asks whether the function lies in the Laguerre-Pólya class D L , and the Thorin-Bondesson programme, which studies the reciprocal as the Laplace transform of a generalised gamma convolution (GGC) and reads the zeros off the Thorin measure. We prove a transfer principle that makes the two programmes a single object. Concretely, to a Laplace exponent Ψ of a spectrally negative Lévy process we attach a van Dantzig function J Ψ , a self-decomposable subordinator T Ψ and a symmetric variable D Ψ = √ 2 B TΨ ; we show that T Ψ is a GGC precisely on the Thorin-Bernstein sub-cone TBF of the Bernstein cone that already carries Ψ, that on this sub-cone the van Dantzig pair [J Ψ , 1/I Ψ ] is exactly a Wald couple, and that J Ψ ∈ D L iff the Thorin measure is supported on (0, ∞) and carried by the squared zeros. The engine is a corrected sine-squared transform that produces the Thorin density in closed form from a Lévy representation; because the kernel is a square, positivity of the Thorin density is automatic when the Lévy measure is positive. For ξ the relevant measure is signed-the archimedean part negative, the prime part positive-so positivity is not automatic but a cancellation, which is exactly where the Riemann hypothesis sits. Applied to the Riemann ξ-function this yields a clean two-tier statement: an unconditional GGC representation of the reciprocal for every base point α > 1, and a conditional reduction of the Riemann hypothesis to the survival of that representation at the critical base point α = 1 2. We compute each zero's contribution to the Thorin measure in closed form-a Lorentzian profile that collapses to an atom at the squared ordinate-and track the residual fractional drift left by the genus-one factors, so that a zero-free half-plane to the right of α is necessary for the reciprocal to be a generalised gamma convolution, and the Riemann hypothesis is the equivalence at α = 1 2. We then isolate the single positivity statement that bears the weight, relate it to the de Bruijn-Newman flow (which moves the Thorin measure, while the Gaussian drift of the symmetric GGC provably cannot move the zeros), and unify the Lukacs and Bondesson closure calculi.

title: The Cost of Listening: AI Advice and Induced Environmental Footprints

detail.title: The Cost of Listening: AI Advice and Induced Environmental Footprints
detail.abstract: AI's environmental footprint can appear in the choices its advice helps produce. This paper develops a theory of the induced environmental footprint of AI advice: the environmental difference between an AI advised choice and the counterfactual choice a user would have made in the relevant non-AI advice environment. Large language models increasingly guide ordinary decisions about travel, food, consumption, household energy, repair, replacement, lawn care, and land use. These decisions often enter AI systems as questions about convenience, cost, speed, quality, uncertainty, or practicality, while their environmental consequences remain in the background. The model treats AI advice as environmental choice architecture that changes perceived payoffs through salience, framing, trust, search costs, ranking, specificity, and confidence. The induced effect arises at the behavioral margin and can move environmental outcomes in either direction, depending on the interaction between the user's frame and the model's default recommendation orientation. AI advice can amplify, dampen, or redirect environmentally consequential choices. The paper distinguishes this behavioral channel from the direct environmental costs of AI operation and outlines staged empirical approaches for measuring it, including recommendation audits, stated-choice experiments, and behavioral or field designs.

title: Against Mandatory Prompt Disclosure in AI-Assisted Scholarship
affiliations: University of Oxford, Queen’s University, University of Oxford - Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics and University of Oxford

detail.title: Against Mandatory Prompt Disclosure in AI-Assisted Scholarship
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming routine as tools for drafting, editing, and revising scholarly manuscripts, raising difficult questions about how much transparency is needed to assess research integrity, authorship, and accountability. In response, some authors have proposed that researchers who use LLMs in manuscript preparation should be required to submit the prompts they used, together with the generated outputs, as supplemental material. We support detailed disclosure when it is needed to assess the scientific validity or reproducibility of a study, for example where LLMs are used in data analysis, coding, literature synthesis, or the production of figures. We argue, however, against Mandatory Full Inclusion (MFI) of prompts and outputs for ordinary writing assistance. Such a policy would, we suggest, be difficult to enforce, easy for dishonest users to evade, burdensome for careful users to follow, and poorly matched to the capacities of editors and peer reviewers. It would also risk discouraging beneficial uses of LLMs, penalising careful multi-model consultation, distorting how researchers interact with AI systems, and disadvantaging scholars who already face undue or unnecessary barriers in academic publishing, including scholars at under-resourced institutions. More generally, an MFI policy would impose a level of surveillance on AI-assisted writing that has no clear analogue in ordinary human collaboration. We propose instead a proportionate prompt-and-output disclosure framework: targeted disclosure where reproducibility or validity requires it; voluntary documentation where authors wish to demonstrate their contribution; and continued reliance on authorship attestation, contributor statements, and misconduct procedures where warranted. This approach better aligns transparency with the risks posed by LLM use in scholarly writing, while also minimising surveillance-related harms and inefficiencies.

title: Hedging Against Climate Change Risk with Trade: Heat Stress and Global Agricultural Markets
affiliations: University of Nebraska at Lincoln, University of Nebraska at Lincoln - Department of Economics, University of Colorado Boulder and University of Colorado at Boulder

detail.title: Hedging Against Climate Change Risk with Trade: Heat Stress and Global Agricultural Markets
detail.abstract: With the large number of empirical estimates of climate change damage, particularly heat stress shocks, and ad hoc recommendations of trade as an adaptation tool in combating climate change, evidence of trade's mitigative effect is relatively scarce. In investigating its role, we find muted trade responses to heat stress shocks, with only one medium-term response to temperature shocks consistent with hedging against future shocks in global agricultural markets. We propose a theoretical optimization framework that highlights risk minimization in import decisions, which suggests that optimal selection of partners and trade shares, reduces supply growth volatility. Empirically however, we find increasing export suppliers is associated with a reduction in price volatilities at the expense of increased supply volatility, while increased external dependence is associated with increased supply volatility and no significant impact on price volatility. Subsequent data calibration and counterfactual analysis points to a higher preference for supply growth maximization as a potential reason for the higher supply volatility observed.

title: Frontier Emerging Technologies, IPO Valuation, and Firm Policies
affiliations: University of Alabama and University of Alabama - Culverhouse College of Commerce & Business Administration

detail.title: Frontier Emerging Technologies, IPO Valuation, and Firm Policies
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic forward-looking measure of an IPO firm’s engagement with frontier emerging technologies (FETech), using textual analysis of its IPO prospectus. Firms with higher FETech exhibit higher first-day returns, greater trading volume, wider bid-ask spreads, and larger price revisions during bookbuilding, consistent with greater valuation uncertainty, stronger information production, and more intensive price discovery. Beyond IPO pricing, higher FETech predicts higher future liquidity, lower leverage, stronger growth, higher valuation, and more intensive post-IPO innovation activity. These effects are not confined to high-tech firms. After controlling for industry effects using Hoberg and Phillips' (2016) textbased network industries (TNIC3) and using a new TNIC3-based procedure to classify firms into high-tech and non-high-tech groups, we show that these effects hold for both groups. Our findings suggest that engaging with leading emerging technologies is a risky but valuable activity for firms.

title: The Forgotten Bridge: Millennials, Lebanese Education, and the Cost of Standing Still

detail.title: The Forgotten Bridge: Millennials, Lebanese Education, and the Cost of Standing Still
detail.abstract: This article examines the structural failures of Lebanon's educational system through the lens of generational equity, with particular focus on the Millennial cohort a generation persistently overlooked in both policy design and institutional reform. Drawing on data from the Association of Banks in Lebanon (ABL), which recorded $240 million in transfers supporting 30,000 Lebanese students studying abroad across the 2019–2021 academic years, the article argues that student emigration is not a symptom of individual preference but of systemic failure to adapt. The article identifies three interconnected deficiencies: the Ministry of Education's resistance to recognizing online degree programs, the absence of flexible learning pathways suited to a crisis-prone environment, and the structural exclusion of Millennials from decision-making roles in educational institutions. Using Saudi Arabia's recent educational reforms as a regional reference point, the article does not advocate wholesale transformation but calls for incremental, evidence-based adaptation. It further argues that Lebanon's Millennial professionals, particularly those working at the intersection of learning, workforce development, and organizational change, represent an underutilized policy resource whose exclusion compounds the very gaps the system fails to address. The article concludes that Lebanon's educational legacy, while historically significant, is insufficient as a substitute for present-day institutional competence and adaptability.

title: Export Quotas Under Joint Mineral Supply: Theory and the DRC Cobalt Shock
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile

detail.title: Export Quotas Under Joint Mineral Supply: Theory and the DRC Cobalt Shock
detail.abstract: Producer-side export quotas are increasingly important in critical-mineral markets that supply the energy transition, but their welfare effects are not necessarily captured by one-commodity supply models. This paper develops a theory of export quotas under joint mineral supply and applies it to the 2026 Democratic Republic of Congo cobalt shock. The model separates official exports from mine output, recovered cobalt, inventories, domestic processing, leakage, strategic reserves, and expiring quota rights. Because cobalt is an input into electric vehicles, stationary storage, portable electronics, and high-performance technologies, the quota also affects energy-transition supply chains. Static results derive a quota-revenue frontier with endogenous offsets. Joint-supply results show how cobalt prices pass through ore output, recovery intensity, and stockpile recovery. Dynamic results show that inventory and curtailment shadow costs raise the optimal quota, while strategic-reserve and domestic-processing value lower it. The calibration treats USD 15/lb as the 2025 annual benchmark and USD 26/lb as a 2026 event price. The current quota lowers official export revenue relative to the no-quota benchmark, but a positive quota can be optimal when retained value on withheld cobalt is sufficiently high. Under the central retained-value calibration, the fiscal optimum is about 110 kt/y, above the current 96.6 kt/y quota. The paper therefore identifies when a price-raising cobalt quota is fiscally attractive, nationally sustainable, and costly for global energy-transition users.

title: Technological Rivalry and the Reorganization of Strategic Trade Networks

detail.title: Technological Rivalry and the Reorganization of Strategic Trade Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary data and does not involve human participants, human subjects, or identifiable personal information. Ethics approval was therefore not required.

detail.abstract: How do geopolitical technology shocks reorganize strategic trade networks? This paper examines whether rising exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) technologies reshapes the geopolitical structure of U.S. supply-chain dependence. I construct new measures of AI-related trade exposure by combining patent-based technology intensity with sectoral trade composition. Using panel fixed-effects models, dynamic event-study specifications, local projection impulse responses, and Bayesian vector autoregressions, I document three findings. First, U.S. AI-related trade net works experienced substantial geopolitical reallocation following the escalation of U.S.-China technological rivalry after 2018. Second, baseline regime-interaction estimates indicate that periods of rising AI exposure were initially associated with greater China-linked import dependence relative to the pre-2016 period. Third, dynamic responses reveal persistent supply-chain adjustment over medium horizons: following AI exposure shocks, China-linked trade dependence gradually declines while diversification toward alternative supplier networks increases. Forecast-error variance decompositions further show that AI exposure shocks explain a substantial share of medium-run fluctuations in strategic trade concentration. Taken together, the findings suggest that technological rivalry reshapes global supply net works through dynamic reorganization rather than static trade contraction alone. The results highlight how strategic technology competition can alter the resilience and diversification structure of modern production networks.

title: Contamination Bias from Adaptation to Environmental Stressors
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder

detail.title: Contamination Bias from Adaptation to Environmental Stressors
detail.abstract: The effects of environmental stressors are likely to vary across individuals, firms, and locations, in part due to adaptation to local conditions. Here, I examine how this relationship between the effects of stressors and the exposure regime can induce important contamination biases if heterogeneity goes unmodeled. For example, failure to model heterogeneity in the impacts of high temperatures can contaminate estimated effects of lower temperatures, or failure to model heterogeneous effects of temperatures could contaminate estimated effects of precipitation. I first show how the conditions for contamination bias can arise using a simple model of adaptation to environmental stress and illustrate the resulting bias with simulations. After detailing a range of solutions, I assess the practical importance of this issue by revisiting published work. I re-analyze links between temperature and asylum applications and crop yields, as well as between drought and migration. Across those settings, contamination bias may inflate effects, dampen them, or alter our understanding of key nonlinearities. Finally, I connect this issue to recent work on related biases.

title: Local Land-Use Regulations: Incentives for Adoption and Desirability of State-Level Override Laws
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Local Land-Use Regulations: Incentives for Adoption and Desirability of State-Level Override Laws
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates both the local incentives to impose supply-restricting local land-use regulations as well as their broader inefficiency, using a theoretical model that is simple and accessible. Although the theme of the paper is somewhat familiar from older work, an updated analysis has value given the striking recent emergence of state-level overrides of local land-use regulations in the US, which the model's social planner would support. These overrides, which are directed at the problem of housing unaffordability, represent an historic phenomenon because regulation of land-use has been the responsibility of local governments in the US for well over a hundred years. As a result, it is important for theoretical analysis to demonstrate their desirability.

title: How IoT Enables Protective Action Decision Model (PADM) During A Wildfire Event

detail.abstract: This article highlights the growing importance of air quality assessment, particularly given the increased frequency and severity of climate-driven wildfires. Recent research suggests that wildfire particulate matter may be more toxic than equivalent amounts of ambient PM2.5, with smoke composition and the different stages of biomass combustion having varying health impacts. This article examines how public managers and decision-makers can use Internet of Things (IoT) devices to make decisions using hyper-local, real-time data on air quality, particularly data on levels of fine particulate matter (PM2.5). We surveyed Oregon residents following the 2020 wildfires, the region's most severe fire season in modern history. We received a total of 1,200 responses from June to August 2021 to help assess how individuals responded to several major wildfires that hit the state in 2020. Results indicate that residents were overwhelmed by the data and were provided with inadequate guidance on how to respond to the dangers posed by the smoke.

detail.abstract: The agricultural industry operates as a complex stochastic service system characterized by high volatility, seasonality, and time-critical operations. Traditional management approaches, often rooted in static strategic controlling, fail to adequately address the probabilistic nature of resource demand and service capacity during peak harvest windows. This article proposes a paradigm shift by modeling agro-industrial enterprises as queueing systems, where machinery and logistics units function as servers and agricultural tasks or harvested commodities function as customers. We develop and analyze specific queueing models - including M/M/1, M/G/k, and finite-source machine repair models - to calculate critical performance metrics such as server utilization, probability of wait, and mean queue length. By transforming qualitative strategic control objectives into quantitative service capacity planning and maintenance optimization problems, this study provides a rigorous mathematical framework for decision-making. Numerical results demonstrate how these models can minimize total expected costs by balancing the cost of service capacity against the economic losses associated with queueing delays. This framework offers a robust, data-driven approach to enhancing the operational resilience and economic viability of modern agribusinesses.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that species-agnostic legal reasoning should refuse species as a dispositive shortcut without becoming species-blind. It develops a legal grammar that moves from anti-speciesist critique to specification: species may orient legal inquiry as defeasible evidence, but law must test what its categories reveal, conceal, and normalize. The paper first shows how ordinary animal-law labels organize legal visibility and can hide inherited judgments about value and harm. It then treats animal worlds as legally salient terrain, drawing on biosemiotics to make habitat, relation, sign-processes, dependency, vulnerability, evidence, and form of life part of legal inquiry. An account of intellectual fields, attention, doctrinal competition, expertise, and controlled publicity explains why animal rightsholding must become conceptually and publicly legible without being captured by charismatic cases, slogans, expert monopoly, rights inflation, or unsafe disclosure. The paper then distinguishes moral status from legal rightsholding by separating moral considerability, protected interests, welfare standards, directed duties, personhood, representation, and rights: moral status opens legal grammar, but a right requires a specified interest, duty-bearer, representative, forum, remedy, evidentiary route, and review mechanism. It concludes with a reviewable protocol for species-agnostic reasoning: audit species and legal classification, identify the animal world, test friction, evidence, and false legibility, fit legal form to the animal interest, specify duty, forum, remedy, and review, preserve the animal's form of life, control representation and publicity, and revise institutions when their first categories fail.

title: From Conflict to Convergence: A Taxonomy of Hybrid Econometric-Deep Learning Architectures for Financial Volatility Forecasting (2019-2026)

detail.title: From Conflict to Convergence: A Taxonomy of Hybrid Econometric-Deep Learning Architectures for Financial Volatility Forecasting (2019-2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to declare.

detail.abstract: Financial volatility forecasting has long been divided between two competing paradigms: the econometric GARCH family, prized for its interpretability and grounding in stylized facts, and deep learning (DL) architectures, prized for their flexibility in capturing high-dimensional nonlinear dependence. This paper provides the first taxonomy-based systematic review of the emerging literature that reconciles these paradigms into hybrid econometric-deep learning architectures. Motivated by the persistent limitations of each approach in isolation-GARCH's rigidity under regime change and high-dimensional inputs, and DL's tendency to overfit and ignore volatility clustering, leverage effects, and fat tails-we argue that the period 2019-2026 constitutes a distinct "convergence window" catalyzed by the Transformer era. Applying PRISMA-style screening criteria to peer-reviewed outlets rated SCI/SSCI Q1/Q2 or ABS 3-star and above, and requiring that eligible studies contain both an explicit econometric volatility component and a deep learning component, we synthesize the literature into three structural paradigms: (A) Pipeline Integration, in which GARCH-derived features feed downstream neural networks; (B) Residual Correction, in which GARCH and DL models operate in parallel and are combined at the output layer; and (C) Parameter Embedding, in which neural networks generate time-varying GARCH parameters within a jointly trained end-to-end system. We find that Paradigm C models consistently deliver the largest and most robust out-of-sample QLIKE and Model Confidence Set gains, particularly during volatile regimes, but at substantial costs to interpretability and computational tractability. We further identify textual sentiment extracted via large language models as the next frontier exogenous driver, particularly within Paradigm C architectures. The review concludes with a research agenda emphasizing standardized benchmarking, regime-aware hybrid design, sentiment-augmented parameter networks, and cross-asset transfer learning.

title: The Impact of High-tech FDI on Labor Market Composition: The Role of Global Value Chains, Vertical Integration, and Intellectual Property
affiliations: Oklahoma State University - Stillwater and

detail.title: The Impact of High-tech FDI on Labor Market Composition: The Role of Global Value Chains, Vertical Integration, and Intellectual Property
detail.abstract: We examine the heterogeneous effects of U.S. outward FDI at various stages of the global value chain (GVC) on the skill composition of labor markets in FDI-destination countries. Existing studies have examined the effects of outsourcing for origin countries, while for FDI-destination countries the focus has either been on the overall effects of FDI inflows or on the effects of GVC participation. Drawing on industry-level FDI data, GVC indicators, and destination-country labor market information, and accounting for fixed effects, our analysis confirms that U.S. FDI generally raises overall skill composition, consistent with prior research. However, we show that investment in more downstream and complex industries reduces the share of highly skilled workers-an effect not previously documented. These findings suggest that the United States retains its most skilled occupations domestically. Thus, our results indicate countervailing effects in FDI-receiving countries which are consistent with the 'hollowing out' of the middle class in developed economies, while simultaneously highlighting the concerns of intellectual property (IP) loss associated with downstream and more technologically complex activities. Countries with stronger intellectual property rights (IPR) protections experience a less pronounced decline in the share of high-skill workers, consistent with reduced IP-related risks.

title: The Silence Penalty: Understanding Introvert-Extravert Wage Differentials
affiliations: Renmin University of China,  and Renmin University of China

detail.title: The Silence Penalty: Understanding Introvert-Extravert Wage Differentials
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether introversion is associated with lower wages in the labor market and whether such differences can be rationalized by sorting, productivity differences, and taste-based discrimination. We develop an equilibrium search-and-bargaining model with search frictions, firm heterogeneity, occupational heterogeneity, and employer taste-based discrimination against introverts. The model predicts that discrimination generates sorting across firms and occupations, a residual wage penalty within the same firm and occupation, and relative productivity-wage differences. Using China Employer-Employee Survey data collected in 2015, 2016, and 2018, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in introversion is associated with an approximately 2.5% decline in hourly wages. Joint estimation of the production function and the wage equation further shows that, relative to their marginal product, introverts are paid less than extraverts. Structural estimation implies a discrimination cost equal to 10.06% of baseline match output. In the estimated model, the discrimination channel accounts for 57.50% of the model-implied wage gap, and eliminating discrimination can increase total welfare by approximately 1.33%. This finding provides micro-level evidence of personality discrimination beyond productivity differences.

title: Retaining Complaining Customers: Understanding Equity-Trust Trade-Offs

detail.abstract: Even customers who invest substantial resources into a relationship with a firm might face a complaint episode and consider whether to switch to another provider. Raising a challenge to the conventional wisdom that suggests increasing relationship investments monotonically lower the risks of complaint-driven consumer churn, the current research identifies another pattern, in which such complaint-driven churn is greatest among customers who invest moderately in their relationships with the firm. The resulting "equity-trust retention curve" follows a U-shaped pattern. To explain it, the authors propose an equity-trust framework that depicts how complaints simultaneously undermine equity and trust, and relationship investments differentially moderate both mechanisms by amplifying equity-based losses but buffering trust erosion. Across both a game-theoretic model and controlled experiments, the findings validate the framework. In turn, applying this framework can enable firms to classify complainers as transactional, switching, or relational and better understand the drivers of their retention.

title: Synthetic Data and Digital Twins: The Hype, The Facts, the Promise
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Marketing

detail.title: Synthetic Data and Digital Twins: The Hype, The Facts, the Promise
detail.abstract: Synthetic data, and in particular digital twins, have captured the interest and imagination of practitioners and academics across disciplines. Indeed, the ability to simulate human behavior and responses in never-seen-before scenarios and questions, using both structured and unstructured data as both input and output, opens powerful possibilities. But a review of the empirical evidence available to date suggests that despite some encouraging results, synthetic data currently do not predict well overall, and systematically distort, human behavior. Many research opportunities exist in improving the accuracy and usefulness of synthetic data and developing novel use cases for digital twins. But researchers and practitioners also need to properly calibrate their expectations of how predictable human behavior is, i.e., on the maximum predictivity achievable by synthetic data.

title: AI-powered Personalized Marketing and Consumer Purchase Decisions: Evidence from Pakistan's e-commerce Sector
affiliations: Bahauddin Zakariya University

detail.title: AI-powered Personalized Marketing and Consumer Purchase Decisions: Evidence from Pakistan's e-commerce Sector
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming e-commerce environments by enabling firms to deliver
AI-powered personalized marketing that enhances consumer engagement and decision efficiency. Despite
growing global interest, limited empirical evidence exists in emerging markets regarding how AI-driven
personalization influences consumer purchase decisions through psychological mechanisms such as trust and
familiarity.
This study examines the impact of AI-powered personalized marketing on consumer purchase decisions in
Pakistan’s e-commerce sector, integrating consumer trust in AI as a mediating variable and consumer familiarity
with AI as a moderating variable. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study extends
traditional TAM by incorporating trust and familiarity as key behavioral determinants in AI-mediated decision
environments.
A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from 300 online consumers using a
structured questionnaire. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyze the
data due to its suitability for complex models involving mediation and moderation, as well as its predictive
orientation.
The results reveal that AI-powered personalized marketing significantly influences consumer purchase decisions
both directly and indirectly through consumer trust in AI. Furthermore, consumer familiarity with AI strengthens
the relationship between trust and purchase decisions, indicating that prior exposure to AI technologies enhances
behavioral responsiveness.
The study contributes to AI marketing literature by extending TAM and providing empirical evidence from an
emerging economy context. Practically, the findings highlight the importance of building t.ransparent, trustworthy,
and user-friendly AI systems to improve consumer adoption and purchase behavior

detail.title: Consumer Dynamics and Vertical Relations: Coordination and Foreclosure in a U.S. Consumer Goods Industry

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Vertical mergers along the supply chain can generate efficiency gains by improving coordination, and anti-competitive harms by disadvantaging rivals. However, the analysis is usually static, limiting our ability to assess recent policy concerns about their dynamic consequences. This paper evaluates how demand-induced dynamics reshape the effects of vertical mergers and uses deep reinforcement learning to overcome the computational challenges. I develop a dynamic model in which downstream firms have multiple suppliers and face dynamic demand, and I train neural networks to approximate the Markov perfect equilibrium. I estimate the model using data from a U.S. consumer goods industry, where habit formation in demand induces strong dynamics. I find that dynamic considerations magnify the consequences of any competitive disadvantage. This prompts firms to moderate their margins, but also strengthens their incentives to disadvantage non-integrated suppliers. Together, these forces produce a perverse outcome: as demand dynamics strengthen, efficiency gains from integration shrink by up to 35% compared to the static case, and integrated firms reduce prices of integrated products by up to 30% less, while foreclosing non-integrated products more severely. Overall, dynamic considerations dampen the pro-competitive effects of vertical mergers and amplify their anti-competitive risks.

title: Liquidization of Skill Capital: The Limit Boundary Shift of Intertemporal Mechanisms in the Age of Technological Acceleration --An Interdisciplinary Extension Based on Adam Smith's Original 1776 Text and Observations of Artificial Intelligence Trajectories
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Liquidization of Skill Capital: The Limit Boundary Shift of Intertemporal Mechanisms in the Age of Technological Acceleration --An Interdisciplinary Extension Based on Adam Smith's Original 1776 Text and Observations of Artificial Intelligence Trajectories
detail.abstract: The intertemporal architecture of modern macroeconomics rests upon an implicit yet pivotal assumption: time serves as a stable, discountable container capable of accommodating the accumulation of human skills through learning and experience to yield intertemporal returns. However, as technological iteration accelerates rapidly through artificial intelligence, multiple phenomena across labor markets, division of labor structures, educational returns, and capital allocation have begun to exhibit characteristics inconsistent with traditional intertemporal frameworks. This study proposes a dual-entrance analytical framework to describe the localized structural shifts in traditional intertemporal mechanisms under limit boundary conditions when technological velocity transcends a specific threshold. The dynamic entrance focuses on the structural divergence between the speed of technological functional absorption and the speed of human cognitive internalization. The static entrance examines the endogenous contraction of the intertemporal certainty window under high frequency technological shocks. Under this framework, skill capital undergoes liquidization, the division of labor exhibits a reversal towards cohesion, educational lag mismatches with instantaneous technological liquidation, capital shifts toward extreme liquidity preferences, and systemic financial risk synchronization intensifies. This paper aims to provide a complementary theoretical perspective for comprehending structural phase transitions in the era of accelerated technology.

title: The Liquidization Of Skill Capital
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Liquidization Of Skill Capital
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a radical reconstruction of macroeconomic and philosophical paradigms regarding labor and human capital under hyper-technological iteration (instantiated by the Artificial Intelligence paradigm shift). We introduce the foundational concept of "Skill Liquidization": when the velocity of technological change crosses a critical threshold, the functional lifespan of human skills approaches zero, mutating skills from Fixed Capital to Liquid Capital due to a near-infinite depreciation rate. This mechanism yields four profound corollaries: (1) The structural collapse of educational investment due to temporal returns mismatch and the non-linear amplification of learning costs; (2) An "Inverse Division of Labor" where task specialization is completely absorbed by intellectual tools, forcing humans into counter-specialization (generalization); (3) The transformation of the traditional proletariat into a sub-proletarian class of "cognitively functional disabled" individuals who lose the capacity for skill-time integration; and (4) The advent of "Consciousness-Centric Productivity," where conscious insight and ideational execution replace physical action as the ultimate economic bottleneck. This paper itself stands as a primary empirical artifact of this paradigm, having been co-authored via direct ideational collaboration with an Artificial Intelligence.

title: Same Occupations, Different Clocks: Separating Remote Work from Generative AI for Labor-Market Entrants

detail.title: Same Occupations, Different Clocks: Separating Remote Work from Generative AI for Labor-Market Entrants
detail.abstract: Is generative AI or remote work behind the weak labor market for new entrants? Separating them is difficult because the occupations language models reach are the same occupations that went remote in 2020. However, the shocks arrived three years apart. I fix CPS entrants' exposure at their pre-pandemic occupation mixes and date each treatment to its own shock. I find a standard deviation of remote-work exposure reduces entry hourly wages by 1.9 percent, a penalty already present for cohorts who entered before ChatGPT launched. I find no detectable wage effect of AI exposure. College employment in AI-exposed occupations falls from the class of 2022, but demographic controls absorb the decline, consistent with reallocation, not a detectable net employment loss.

detail.abstract: This study examines the effects of ordinal weight rank on students' mental health and academic performance. Using nationally representative data from Chinese middle school students randomly assigned to classes, we exploit quasi-random variation in the distribution of students' body weights across classes within the same school and grade to identify causal effects. We find that students with a higher ordinal weight rank have poorer mental health and lower test scores. We further show that these effects are driven by reduced self-confidence, diminished future expectations, lower study effort, and worse school belonging, rather than differences in parental human capital investments or teacher-student interactions. We also provide evidence that frequent communication between parents and children is likely to mitigate the negative effects of ordinal weight rank.

detail.abstract:
Brands increasingly seek growth by identifying the right consumers, understanding where future demand is likely to emerge, and allocating marketing and commercial resources more efficiently. Recent advances in quick commerce, retail media, data clean rooms, Data Exchange models, first-party data systems, and transaction or mobility partnerships are making this increasingly possible in digitally observable environments. For Indian consumer packaged goods (CPG) brands, however, this opportunity remains structurally incomplete. Digital commerce provides identity-rich, SKU-level, timestamped, and address-linked buyer truth, but it captures only a limited share of the market. The majority of CPG demand continues through general trade, kiranas, distributors, and fragmented modern trade, where brands usually lack deterministic consumer-level purchase visibility. 
Existing marketing analytics research has advanced segmentation, CRM, media response, marketing mix modelling, and causal measurement in data-rich environments. However, limited theoretical or practical work explains how a CPG brand can identify its offline-relevant consumers beyond first-party and digitally observed buyers, estimate their incremental commercial contribution rather than only their purchase propensity, and validate value when user-level offline attribution is unavailable. This paper proposes the Unified Audience Graph as a privacy-safe, executable, and mathematically specified framework for addressing this gap. The framework integrates Digital Buyer Signatures, Survey-calibrated Offline Correction, Availability-adjusted Offline Propensity Scores, Expected Incremental Value, and Audience-Weighted Media Pressure into a single operating model. It answers four linked questions: who the brand's offline-relevant consumers are likely to be, where those consumers are commercially actionable, which cohorts are expected to add incremental value, and whether activation produces measurable market uplift. The contribution is a CPG-specific Proof-of-Value framework that shifts audience strategy from digital audience construction and deterministic attribution claims toward offline demand inference, consumer-market opportunity identification, incremental-value prioritisation, and causal market-level validation.

title: Social Learning from AI-Generated Review Summaries
affiliations: Wisconsin School of Business, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, Carnegie Mellon University and College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Social Learning from AI-Generated Review Summaries
detail.abstract: AI-generated review summaries are increasingly popular across digital platforms, where agentic AI modules ingest review histories and autonomously decide which aspects of a product to surface for future customers. We study how the design of such summaries shapes social learning in markets for multi-attribute experience goods. We compare three review systems: a traditional system that displays average ratings, a baseline AI-summary system that compresses past reviews into selected components, and a debiased AI-summary system that we propose. We show that, while traditional ratings lead customers to form the same belief about unknown product quality, the baseline AI-summary system enables personalized learning-different customers infer different valuations from the same summary-but introduces a persistent algorithmic compression bias: by selecting summary components to explain variation in past buyer preferences, the AI systematically omits quality-relevant attributes whenever the dimensions of greatest preference variation differ from the dimensions of true product quality. This bias is asymmetric: it falls disproportionately on customers whose preferences are underrepresented among past buyers. Our debiased AI-summary system constrains compression to preserve the platform's current quality estimate. Under this design, customer beliefs converge almost surely to their true valuations. When the platform sets a price endogenously, debiased AI-summaries can raise both optimal price and profit relative to the traditional system, provided the product's quality profile is sufficiently aligned with average customer preferences.

detail.abstract: Modern agribusiness operates in a volatile globalized economy characterized by rapid technological advancement, shifting consumer preferences, and strict constraints imposed by the biological properties of perishable agricultural products. While traditional management literature treats marketing strategies and logistics optimization as distinct functional areas, this study posits that their independent operation inevitably leads to supply chain congestion, inventory spoilage, and reduced customer service levels. This paper proposes a revision of the strategic integration of marketing and logistics through the lens of Queueing Theory. We conceptualize marketing efforts as the primary driver of the order arrival rate (lambda), and logistics capacity as the determinant of the service rate (mu). By applying Little's Law and stochastic modeling to perishable inventory systems, we quantify the trade-offs between demand generation and throughput capacity. Unlike previous studies utilizing multi-criteria decision-making tools such as AHP or TOPSIS, this paper employs analytical queueing models to demonstrate that uncoordinated increases in marketing intensity without corresponding logistics adjustments lead to exponential growth in congestion costs and product loss. Results indicate that dynamic synchronization of lambda and mu, enabled by digital technologies and predictive analytics, is essential for maintaining system stability (rho less than 1) and maximizing agribusiness profitability.

detail.title: When Do Promotions Cannibalize and When They Complement? A Theoretical and Empirical Investigation
detail.abstract: Promotion spillover is predominantly complementary in traditional retail, with prior research documenting that most promotions generate positive cross-product spillovers. We show that in community group buying (CGB), a retail format where social endorsements and time-constrained ordering replace free browsing, this complementarity reverses and cannibalization dominates across most categories. We develop a two-type heterogeneous consumer nested logit model distinguishing targeted shoppers (who substitute within categories) and browsing shoppers (who generate cross-category traffic), identifying browsing entry elasticity (τ) as the structural boundary between cannibalization and complementarity regimes. Using 775,584 store-day-SKU observations from a leading Chinese CGB platform, we confirm the dominance of cannibalization and validate all four theoretical propositions. Structural simulations show that τ-informed promotion strategies yield substantial profit gains.

title: Measuring the Value of Disability Insurance from Take-Up Decisions

detail.title: Measuring the Value of Disability Insurance from Take-Up Decisions
detail.abstract: The central trade-off for designing Disability Insurance (DI) is between providing insurance to those in need while maintaining incentives to work. This paper develops a novel revealed-preference approach to identify the insurance value of DI benefits. We show that comparing the DI take-up response to a change in benefits versus a change in wages identifies the insurance value. Implementing our framework in Canada, we estimate that increasing DI benefits by $1 creates an additional disincentive cost of $0.60 but creates an insurance value of $2.20. Thus, our approach suggests that DI benefits are not overly generous in the Canadian context.

title: Identity Uncertainty
affiliations: University of California, Davis, Duke University, University of British Columbia (UBC) - Vancouver School of Economics and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Identity Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Many group identities that influence economic behavior are imperfectly observed. Individuals and institutions often conceal identity markers to limit discrimination. Yet concealment also creates uncertainty about group membership, hampering coordination in social interaction. To study this tradeoff, we paired high- and low-caste men for collaborative data entry work in North India. We randomly assigned each mixed-caste pair to either be: (i) introduced by full names, making caste common knowledge; (ii) introduced by first names only, making caste disclosure a choice; or (iii) instructed not to disclose caste. The two concealment conditions substantially reduce the accuracy of beliefs about a partner’s caste and confidence in those beliefs. They also weaken workplace relations, lowering trust, willingness to interact, and perceived productivity—consistent with identity helping structure social coordination. Evidence on mechanisms shows that identity concealment inhibits authentic interaction, making workers less able to express their “true selves,” while certainty about a partner’s identity is associated with stronger workplace ties. Concealment leaves a sizable caste disparity in higher-status role assignment intact, suggesting minimal impacts on discrimination. We conclude that where group identities are socially entrenched, reducing their legibility may undermine intergroup relations.

title: The Robustness and Effectiveness of Nearest Neighbour Distributions as a Measure of Cell Type Co-Localisation in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
affiliations: University of Queensland, University of Queensland, University of Queensland, Wesley Research Institute, Mater Hospital Brisbane, Queensland University of Technology, University of Queensland, University of Queensland and University of Queensland

detail.title: The Robustness and Effectiveness of Nearest Neighbour Distributions as a Measure of Cell Type Co-Localisation in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
detail.abstract: Recent advances in spatial biology have presented an unprecedented ability to investigate transcript or proteomic data at a cellular level. A key area of interest is how the addition of spatial context can be used to investigate compositional differences or cell-to-cell interactions for use as prognostic biomarkers. One method to quantitatively measure these interactions is the area under the curve (AUC) of the G-cross function. While many spatial biology papers have used this metric to investigate specific interactions, an all-interaction approach may be required for more robust biomarker discovery. Additionally, there are several theoretical corrections that can be made to this metric, to measure a reliable biological interaction. Thus, we sort to investigate the effect of edge corrections, rare cell types, sample inhomogeneity, compartmentalisation, and missing value imputation on G-cross AUC and its alternative form, the F-function. This was done using a combination of simulation studies and a real-world non-small cell tissue microarray dataset to validate the theoretical corrections. In terms of edge corrections, we recommend either the Kaplan-Meier or a combination of the Border or Hanisch corrections as these were found to be most applicable to cell data. Additionally, G-cross AUC was found to be heavily influenced by rare cell count with shorter range interactions requiring more cells to prevent spurious value detection. Relaxing the assumption of a homogeneous distribution of cells, by using an inhomogeneous G-cross AUC was found to be complicated by estimation of the intensity function. Finally, computing a compartmentalised G-cross AUC was found to bias between-cell distances, when using a biologically derived compartment. We developed a new open-source package, PyGcross, providing a pythonic entry point for the G-cross computation.

title: Label and Compute-Efficient Chest X-ray Diagnosis with BYOL Against SimCLR

detail.title: Label and Compute-Efficient Chest X-ray Diagnosis with BYOL Against SimCLR
detail.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become the principal route to reducing the expert-annotation burden that limits deep learning for chest-radiograph (CXR) interpretation, yet the dominant contrastive paradigm couples accuracy to large batches of negative pairs, inflating the memory and compute that under-resourced clinics can least afford. This paper proposes and rigorously evaluates a non-contrastive SSL framework based on Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) for CXR diagnosis, and benchmarks it against SimCLR, MoCo~v2, SimSiam, and a fully supervised baseline. The study is framed around two efficiency axes that prior CXR-SSL work reports only in isolation (label efficiency and compute/scale efficiency) and a third, often-omitted axis of statistical soundness. We formalize the BYOL objective for the medical-imaging setting, derive its collapse-avoidance behavior, and define a scale-efficiency protocol that quantifies accuracy as a function of the labeled-data fraction, pre-training compute budget, and batch size. Across three public datasets (NIH ChestX-ray14, CheXpert, and the Kaggle CXR-Pneumonia corpus), the framework attains higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) at every label budget, with the largest gains in the low-label regime (1 - 10%). In a controlled comparison at 10% labels, BYOL improves CheXpert AUROC by Delta=0.031 over SimCLR (paired bootstrap 95% confidence interval [0.029,0.033], p<0.001) and reaches a fixed operating point with roughly 8x less pre-training computation (16 vs. 128 GPU-hours). The results indicate that non-contrastive SSL is a hardware-democratizing route to label-efficient CXR diagnosis and is extensible to other radiology modalities.

title: Ports, Technology and Inter-City Trade: The Economics and Geopolitics of Evolving Maritime Transport Networks
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC), Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF) - Centre de Recerca en Economia Internacional (CREI), Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) and University of Oregon - Department of Economics

detail.title: Ports, Technology and Inter-City Trade: The Economics and Geopolitics of Evolving Maritime Transport Networks
detail.abstract: Maritime transport remains the backbone of global trade, yet the port and shipping network that carries it has been transformed by containerization and related technological advances. Drawing on newly available granular data — digitized historical shipping records, georeferenced ship movements, and shipment-level routing information — we present five stylized facts on the structure and evolution of the maritime network. Global shipping activity is highly concentrated among a changing lineup of dominant top ports even as lower-ranked ports disperse, while state-owned Chinese port terminal operators increasingly account for these global volumes, boosting overall port operations while delivering efficiency gains mostly to Chinese vessels. We use these facts to organize a synthesis of a fast-growing literature: containerization reshaped which port cities could expand, reinforced hub-and-spoke concentration that yields large but localized welfare gains, embedded ports in multimodal networks that amplify the returns to infrastructure, and generated market power, congestion, and environmental costs. Together, this evidence shows how evolving maritime technologies simultaneously deepen global integration and heighten the economic and geopolitical importance of critical nodes in the transport network — and of who controls them.

title: Job Ads as Signals: Evidence from a Priced Amenity and Worker Beliefs
affiliations: University of Oxford, Regent's Park College, Bank of England, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), IZA and Cornell  University,  Ithaca,  New  York

detail.title: Job Ads as Signals: Evidence from a Priced Amenity and Worker Beliefs
detail.abstract: Discrete choice experiments are widely used to estimate workers' willingness to pay (WTP) for job amenities under the assumption that varying an attribute does not change workers' beliefs about other job attributes. We test this assumption by embedding an amenity with a known market price — a popular monthly public transport pass — in a large-scale discrete choice experiment with German workers. Many workers, including public transport users, overvalue the ticket by more than 100%, despite WTP for other attributes aligning with the literature. A complementary belief-elicitation experiment shows that advertising an amenity, such as the pass but also common amenities like work from home, causally shifts beliefs about unlisted attributes of the job. Posted wages similarly signal unlisted attributes so that wage variation, the money metric for WTP calculation, is itself contaminated by belief spillovers — such as higher pay signaling heightened stress. These spillovers imply that discrete choice estimates capture perceived bundles rather than isolated attributes, and distort current estimates of non-wage compensation and monopsony power.

title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
affiliations: Utah State University - Huntsman School of Business, Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business - Economics Department and Oesterreichische Nationalbank (Eurosystem)

detail.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
detail.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden antiGerman backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock.
